docs/research/a100_latency_sweep.py.doc:
Run the ptxas-derived fixed-pipe latency sweep entirely under docs/research/.

This invokes the existing SASS encoder/emulator and GPU runner, but patches only
their output roots to docs/research/a100-latency/corpus/. It measures each
producer/consumer SASS dependency at producer stalls 1..8 (predicate guards
1..15) against the emulator on a real A100.

    modal run docs/research/a100_latency_sweep.py --trials 2 --budget 300

docs/research/a100_mma_tensorcore.py.doc:
Modal experiment: fused rank-7 matrix multiplication on an A100.

Run from the repository root:
    modal run docs/research/a100_mma_tensorcore.py         --shapes 4096x4096x4096,4096x4096x16384,16384x4096x4096

The experiment compares cuBLAS, a one-kernel Triton GEMM, and one-kernel fused
Strassen / AlphaTensor 2x2x2 schemes. It emits PTX and nvdisasm SASS only below
docs/research/a100-mma-artifacts/ and a JSON report next to this script.

symbols.name: bilinear_gemm
symbols.doc: One CTA computes corresponding tiles of all four C quadrants.

examples/mlp/kernels.py.doc:
A 2-layer MLP forward pass (linear -> ReLU -> linear) -- the feed-forward
block inside a transformer layer, minus attention/softmax/layernorm (those
need exp/transcendentals, which openassembler.pyfront and our backend don't
support yet; see docs/STATUS.md "Gaps"). Every kernel here compiles through
openassembler.pyfront's small Python subset straight to our own SASS backend --
no ptxas code generation anywhere in this pipeline.

Shapes: x (batch x in_dim), W1 (in_dim x hidden), b1 (hidden),
        W2 (hidden x out_dim), b2 (out_dim), out (batch x out_dim).
One thread computes one output element (row, col) of its layer -- naive,
not tiled/blocked like openassembler.fastmm's GEMM kernels, which is the honest
trade for writing it in ~10 lines of Python instead of hand-tuned PTX.

linear1/linear2 launch a 2D grid: ctaid.x = row (one block per batch row,
as before), ctaid.y * ntid.x + tid.x = col -- so hidden/out_dim can exceed
CUDA's 1024-thread-per-block limit (tools/mlp_run.py picks ntid.x and
ctaid.y's count to cover hidden/out_dim between them).

    openassembler compile examples/mlp/kernels.py --kernel linear1 -o linear1.cubin

examples/nn_ops.py.doc:
Small correctness/measurement baselines, not tuned production NN kernels.

Use tools/nn_study.py to compile, validate and measure each operation. Each output
is overwritten on every invocation so repeated timing does not mutate its inputs.

examples/transformer_training.py.doc:
train_transformer.py
====================

A fairly complete, from-scratch training pipeline for a decoder-only
Transformer language model.

Features
--------
* Character-level tokenizer (trivially swappable for BPE)
* Pre-norm Transformer blocks with RMSNorm
* Rotary position embeddings (RoPE)
* SwiGLU feed-forward network
* Fused attention via torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention
* Weight tying between embedding and LM head
* KV-cache for fast autoregressive sampling
* AdamW with decoupled weight decay + parameter grouping
* Cosine LR schedule with linear warmup
* Mixed precision (bf16 or fp16 + GradScaler)
* Gradient accumulation and gradient clipping
* Checkpointing / resuming
* Deterministic seeding
* Sampling with temperature / top-k / top-p
* Optional torch.compile

Usage
-----
    python train_transformer.py                        # synthetic demo corpus
    python train_transformer.py --data_path my.txt     # train on your own text
    python train_transformer.py --compile --max_steps 5000

examples/vector_add.py.doc:
Minimal openassembler.pyfront example: elementwise vector add, compiled from a
small Python subset straight to SASS by our own backend -- no ptxas code
generation involved (see README.md "How it works").

    openassembler compile examples/vector_add.py -o out.cubin --dump-ptx

This isn't general Python: openassembler.pyfront accepts a small, explicitly
scoped numeric subset (typed params, for-range loops, if/else, arithmetic,
array indexing, and a few GPU intrinsics) -- see openassembler/pyfront/__init__.py
for exactly what's supported.

openassembler/__init__.py.doc:
OpenAssembler: a Python / CUDA C / C++ (and PTX) to NVIDIA SASS compiler with its own
backend, built on from-scratch reverse engineering of the Volta+ 128-bit SASS ISA.

openassembler/backend/__init__.py.doc: Backend: instruction selection, register assignment, scheduling, encoding.

openassembler/backend/compile.py.doc:
M3 v0: naive PTX -> SASS compiler for straight-line probe kernels (sm_80).

Pipeline: parse PTX -> select SASS per PTX instruction -> assign one physical
register per PTX virtual register (no reuse; the probes are tiny) -> conservative
scheduling (control bits from the mined model, scoreboards for every variable-
latency op) -> template encoder -> splice into a ptxas-built cubin of the same
kernel (we reuse its ELF/.nv.info skeleton and fix REGCOUNT and EXIT offsets).

Coverage is deliberately small. Unsupported PTX raises NotSupported.
Includes our own strength reduction: div/rem by an immediate uses the exhaustively
proved multiply-high sequences from openassembler.opt.divconst.

symbols.name: schedule
symbols.doc:
In-order, no reordering.
* Variable-latency writes (loads, S2R): write scoreboard; readers and over-writers wait.
* Memory ops read their source registers asynchronously: read scoreboard; later
  writers of those registers wait (WAR) - required once registers are reused.
* Control flow: scoreboard state is not tracked across joins, so the instruction at
  every label and every branch waits on all outstanding scoreboards.
* Fixed-latency results:
    model="safe"   stall 6 after every op (above every latency mined from ptxas)
    model="mined"  stall = exact distance to the next dependent consumer, using the
                   per-class minimum latencies mined from ptxas (tools/mine_latency.py
                   -> corpus/sm_80/machine_model.json) plus the mined issue gaps.

symbols.name: _branch_pred_latency
symbols.doc:
An instruction guarded by @Px reads Px at issue: on the A100 a guard 6..12 cycles
after its ISETP/FSETP used the OLD predicate (loops ran one extra iteration; guarded
IADD3/IMAD/FADD kept stale results), while the emulator, which has no timing, was
right. Measured minimum: 13 cycles for every guarded opcode tried. A predicate read as
a source operand (SEL ..., P0) needs only 4. Enforce 13 by raising stalls.

symbols.name: hw_latency
symbols.doc:
RAW latency (cycles) from fixed-latency `prod` to `cons` (opcode names). Falls back
to 6 for producers outside the measured pipes. Exceptions measured on the A100:
FMNMX (alu) -> FADD (fma) is 5 like any cross-pipe pair.

symbols.name: _mined_stalls
symbols.doc:
Replace the fixed stall-6 with distance-to-next-dependent-consumer, using the
mined minimum latency of each producer class (and per-pair when known).
Conservative where the model has no data: falls back to 6.

openassembler/backend/fragments.py.doc:
ptxas's own SASS sequences for PTX ops we don't hand-select (IEEE div/rcp/sqrt, the
.approx MUFU wrappers, integer div/rem by a register, f32<->int cvt with rounding).

Why copy ptxas instead of writing our own: these sequences encode numerical facts
(Newton steps around an approximate MUFU, FCHK's slow-path trigger, the I2F.RP/F2I
reciprocal trick with its two fix-up steps, the scale-by-2^24 denormal wrappers) that
are only "right" because they match NVIDIA's implementation bit for bit. Copying is the
project rule ("never guess"), and the copy is checked against ptxas's own SASS for the
same probe on the emulator (tests/test_backend_ops.py).

Data: ptxas_fragments.json, generated from CUDA 12.8 probes. Each record
contains inputs (original register -> source index), output, renamed-label-ready
lines, and the original PTX/SASS for independent regression replay. Arithmetic
helpers are flattened to branches; registers and predicates are private at each
use site. No NVIDIA toolkit binaries or source files are packaged.

symbols.name: roles
symbols.doc:
-> (guard, opcode, operands, kinds) with kinds[i] in
{"rd", "ru", "pd", "pu", None}: register def/use, predicate def/use, other.

symbols.name: lower_line
symbols.doc:
One fragment SASS line -> (fmt, defs, uses, guard, target) for ra.Op, with
reg(n) / pred(n) mapping ptxas register / predicate numbers to virtual ones.
fmt uses {dK}/{sK} for register defs/uses, {pK} for predicate defs, {qK} for
predicate uses (the negation travels in the use tuple, (PV, neg)), {target} for
a branch label. `.reuse` is dropped (our scheduler sets reuse bits itself).

symbols.name: reads_writes
symbols.doc: (register numbers read, written, predicates read, written) of one fragment line.

openassembler/backend/naive.py.doc:
M3 v0 (kept for A/B comparison): naive PTX -> SASS compiler, one register per PTX vreg.

Pipeline: parse PTX -> select SASS per PTX instruction -> assign one physical
register per PTX virtual register (no reuse; the probes are tiny) -> conservative
scheduling (control bits from the mined model, scoreboards for every variable-
latency op) -> template encoder -> splice into a ptxas-built cubin of the same
kernel (we reuse its ELF/.nv.info skeleton and fix REGCOUNT and EXIT offsets).

Coverage is deliberately small. Unsupported PTX raises NotSupported.
Includes our own strength reduction: div/rem by an immediate uses the exhaustively
proved multiply-high sequences from openassembler.opt.divconst.

symbols.name: schedule
symbols.doc:
In-order, no reordering. Fixed-latency ALU results: stall so the next reader
is >= 6 cycles later (above every fixed latency mined from ptxas, max 5-6 for
IMAD.WIDE/LEA). Variable-latency ops get a write scoreboard; readers wait on it.

openassembler/backend/ra.py.doc:
M3 v1: PTX -> SASS with a virtual-register IR, copy elimination, and linear-scan
register allocation (sm_80, straight-line kernels).

Pipeline
  select()    PTX -> IR over virtual registers. PTX moves are renamings (no code);
              kernel params stay c[0x0][...] operands; (mul.wide + add.s64) becomes
              one IMAD.WIDE; v4/v2 vectors become "groups" that must get consecutive,
              aligned physical registers.
  dce()       drop instructions whose results are never used (and have no side effect).
  allocate()  linear scan over live intervals; groups (64/128-bit values) get
              aligned consecutive registers; a group member defined by a plain copy
              is coalesced into its slot so the copy disappears.
  lower()     IR -> SASS text with physical registers (feeds compile.schedule + encoder).

Every unsupported construct raises NotSupported; nothing is guessed.

symbols.name: V
symbols.doc: A 32-bit virtual register.

symbols.name: C
symbols.doc: c[0x0][off] operand (kernel params, launch constants).

symbols.name: I
symbols.doc: 32-bit immediate.

symbols.name: Op
symbols.doc:
One SASS instruction over virtual registers.

fmt:   SASS text with {d0} {d1}.. for defs and {s0} {s1}.. for uses
defs:  list of tuples of V; a tuple of length 2/4 must be consecutive, aligned regs
uses:  same, for sources (V, C, I or tuples of V for wide sources)
side:  has an effect besides its defs (store, exit) -> never removed by DCE
var_lat: variable latency (needs a write scoreboard)

symbols.name: PV
symbols.doc: A virtual predicate register (allocated to P0..P6).

symbols.name: _flat
symbols.doc:
Registers referenced by defs/uses: expands register groups, skips predicate
operands ((PV, neg) tuples and bare PV).

symbols.name: dce
symbols.doc: Remove ops whose defs are never used and that have no side effect.

symbols.name: cfg_liveness
symbols.doc:
live_out[i] for each op (set of V/PV live right after op i), by iterating
dataflow to a fixpoint over the op-level CFG (fallthrough + branch targets).
A guarded op does not kill its defs (it may not execute).

symbols.name: coalesce
symbols.doc:
Delete copies `d <- s` that feed a wide operand, by renaming d to s, when s can
live in d's register slot: s is a scalar (in no other group), not already
coalesced into another slot, and not a member of the same tuple twice.

symbols.name: _intervals
symbols.doc:
[first, last] op index where each V is defined, used, or live (CFG liveness),
so values carried around a loop's back edge stay allocated for the whole loop.

symbols.name: _alloc
symbols.doc:
Linear scan over groups in start order. A register is free for value v if
the previous value in it ended at or before v's start: a value last read by an
instruction may share a register with that instruction's result (operands are
read before results are written; ptxas does this too, e.g. IMAD.WIDE R4, R4, ..).

symbols.name: allocate
symbols.doc:
Allocate, then re-allocate with copy-affinity hints (a copy's source prefers its
destination's register) until no improvement; keep the allocation that leaves the
fewest real copies.

symbols.name: allocate_preds
symbols.doc: PV -> P0..P6 by interval coloring (same interval rule as registers).

symbols.name: lower
symbols.doc:
-> [(text, var_lat, reads, writes)] with physical registers. Labels become
("<label>", ...) markers resolved by compile_kernel's branch encoding.

symbols.name: compile_kernel
symbols.doc: PTX kernel -> (sass texts with control bits, stats). Uses the v0 scheduler.

symbols.name: encode_code
symbols.doc: Encode scheduled code; branches get their target address from `labels`.

symbols.name: bind
symbols.doc: PTX register `name` := v. For home registers, emit a real copy into the home.

symbols.name: wide
symbols.doc:
A tuple used as a wide (consecutive-register) operand. If no single op
defines exactly this tuple, copy members into a fresh group; coalesce()
later deletes every copy that has no real register conflict.

symbols.name: reg32
symbols.doc: Operand that must be a register (materialize c[]/imm with a MOV).

symbols.name: fragment
symbols.doc: Expand a validated arithmetic sequence into private virtual registers.

symbols.name: pred
symbols.doc: PTX predicate operand -> (PV, negated).

openassembler/backend/sched.py.doc:
Basic-block list scheduler: reorders lowered instructions before control bits are set.

Input/output: [(text, var_lat, reads, writes)] with physical registers and "<label X>"
markers (openassembler.backend.ra.lower). Within each block (labels and branches end blocks)
instructions are reordered by critical path, using the A100-measured latencies
(compile.hw_latency, corpus/sm_80/hw_latency.json):
  * register RAW / WAR / WAW, predicate def/use (a @P guard needs 13 cycles),
  * memory ops and barriers keep their relative order (no alias analysis),
  * ULDC.64 UR4 (the global-memory descriptor) precedes every memory op,
  * the block's final BRA/EXIT/RET stays last.

openassembler/backend/unroll.py.doc:
PTX-level unrolling of counted do-while loops (the shape ptxas also unrolls 4x).

Recognized loop (no other labels/branches inside, %c not written by B, %n loop-invariant):

    L:  B;  add.u32 %c, %c, 1;  setp.lt.u32 %p, %c, %n;  @%p bra L;

Rewritten (B runs exactly as often as before; %p is false at the exit as before):

        B; inc                                    first iteration (do-while)
        setp.lt.u32 %p, %c, %n;  @!%p bra DONE
        sub.u32 %t, %n, %c;  setp.lt.u32 %q, %t, U;  @%q bra TAIL     # %t = iterations left
    MAIN: (B; inc) x U;  sub.u32 %t, %n, %c;  setp.ge.u32 %q, %t, U;  @%q bra MAIN
          (if B does not read %c:  add %c, U; setp.lt %q, %c, %n-(U-1); B x U; @%q bra MAIN)
        setp.lt.u32 %p, %c, %n;  @!%p bra DONE
    TAIL: B; inc;  setp.lt.u32 %p, %c, %n;  @%p bra TAIL
    DONE:

Correctness is checked per kernel by the caller (emulator vs PTX interpreter on the
original kernel).

openassembler/build.py.doc:
`openassembler compile` (and the compile half of `cnr`): source file or source
tree -> output/ (layout and manifest schema: openassembler.project).

Per source file:
  1. frontend: .ptx as-is, .py via openassembler.pyfront, .cu/.cpp via nvcc --ptx
     (openassembler.frontend.to_ptx_module) -> ONE PTX module with all its kernels
  2. our backend (openassembler.backend.ra) generates every kernel's SASS; --verify
     checks each on the SASS emulator against the PTX reference interpreter
  3. ptxas -O3 builds the same PTX (restricted to the kernels that will be in the
     cubin) once: that cubin is both the ELF container we splice our code into and
     the reference `openassembler run` compares against (.build/reference/)
  4. each kernel's .text is spliced into that one container; a kernel our backend
     can't compile is an error, or with --fallback ptxas keeps ptxas's code -- said
     so in the manifest, the .sass header and the summary, never silently
  5. nvdisasm lists the final cubin -> sass/<name>.sass (and re-reads every word we
     encoded as a sanity check)

Multi-kernel cubins: container.cubin.splice_text, applied once per kernel, rewrites
EVERY EIATTR_REGCOUNT record in .nv.info with that kernel's count (it was written
for one-kernel probes). The last splice would win for all kernels, so a kernel
needing more registers than the last one would be launched with too few and fault
(CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION, see required_regcount's evidence). splice_kernels
below re-fixes each REGCOUNT record by its function's symbol index after splicing.

symbols.name: _show
symbols.doc: A path as the user would type it: relative to the cwd when under it.

symbols.name: encoder
symbols.doc:
One Encoder per arch per process (loading its templates is the slow part).
Raises EncodeError("no SASS encoder data for ...") for an arch we have no data for.

symbols.name: generate
symbols.doc:
One PTX kernel -> (code, labels, words, exits, nregs) with our backend. Raises
ra.NotSupported / EncodeError for what it can't do (never guesses).

symbols.name: verify_kernel
symbols.doc:
("ok" | "failed" | "not-verified", message). Picks the original fixed
probe-ABI harness for probe-shaped kernels (out/in/k/kf -- the corpus this
repo's own tests use), or the generic one (openassembler.verify) for anything
else, which covers pyfront/cppfront kernels and hand-written PTX with any
signature.

symbols.name: restrict_ptx
symbols.doc:
The same PTX module with every .entry not in `keep` removed (its whole
declaration and body), so ptxas builds a container with exactly the kernels that
go into the cubin. Device functions, globals and the header stay untouched.

symbols.name: splice_kernels
symbols.doc:
Splice several kernels' code (name -> (words, nregs, exits)) into one ptxas
container. Kernels not in `ours` keep ptxas's code and its register count.

symbols.name: regcounts
symbols.doc: kernel name -> registers as the driver will see them (.nv.info REGCOUNT).

symbols.name: _scratch_tool
symbols.doc:
Run fn(path) on a scratch copy of `data` under the repo (on macOS the toolkit
runs in a VM that only sees $HOME, wherever the output folder is).

symbols.name: ptxas_build
symbols.doc: ptxas -O3 (its default) on a PTX module -> cubin bytes.

symbols.name: split_listing
symbols.doc: nvdisasm output of a multi-kernel cubin -> {kernel: that .text section's lines}.

symbols.name: sanity_check_listing
symbols.doc:
Soft check, never fatal: every non-branch instruction nvdisasm printed should
be the one we encoded (branch targets are renamed by nvdisasm, so those lines
legitimately differ, and nvdisasm prints an f32 immediate we wrote as raw bits,
FADD R3, R3, 0x3f800000, as its value, 1). Returns a warning or None.

symbols.name: listing_insn_count
symbols.doc:
Instructions in a ptxas-built section, counted like count_insns: no NOP padding,
no trailing self-branch.

symbols.name: c_param_names
symbols.doc:
kernel -> its parameter names as written in CUDA C. nvcc's PTX names them
<kernel>_param_<i>, which hides that the last one is `n`; `openassembler run`'s
auto-harness uses these to give n/count/size-named ints the element count.
Best effort (extern "C" kernels; templates and macros are simply not matched).

symbols.name: build_source
symbols.doc:
Compile one source file into in-memory outputs (SourceOut.files); nothing is
written here. `single`: a --kernel that isn't in this file is an error (in a repo
it just means this file has nothing to build).

symbols.name: _brief
symbols.doc: The informative line of a (possibly multi-line, nvcc) error, for one-line summaries.

symbols.name: compile_paths
symbols.doc:
`openassembler compile SRC`: a file or a directory. Returns the exit code and what
was written (cnr runs exactly those kernels).

openassembler/cli.py.doc:
OpenAssembler 0.2.0: a Python / CUDA C / C++ (and PTX) to NVIDIA SASS compiler with its own backend.

    openassembler compile kernel.py|kernel.cu|kernel.ptx [-o NAME] [--verify]   # -> output/cubin + output/sass
    openassembler compile my_repo/                    # every kernel in a repo, mirrored into output/
    openassembler run [output] [--backend local|modal|user@host] [--dry-run]   # ours vs ptxas on a GPU
    openassembler cnr SRC [compile + run options]     # compile, then run what compiled
    openassembler status                              # headline results (docs/STATUS.md)
    openassembler corpus | check | bench | fastmm | gpu run   # research tooling (tools/*.py)
    openassembler                                     # no arguments: interactive shell

Frontends turn each source into PTX (.py: openassembler.pyfront; .cu/.cpp: nvcc --ptx);
our backend generates the SASS and splices it into a ptxas-built ELF container (README.md
"How it works"). Run `openassembler <command> --help` for every flag.

symbols.name: _run_tool
symbols.doc: Exec tools/<script> with the same interpreter, PYTHONPATH=ROOT.

symbols.name: cmd_compile
symbols.doc:
Source file or directory -> output/ (cubin/, sass/, manifest.json, .build/),
using our backend (openassembler.backend.ra) instead of ptxas's code generator.
Accepts .ptx (as-is), .py (openassembler.pyfront's numeric subset), or
.cu/.cuh/.cpp/.cc/.cxx (via nvcc --ptx, openassembler.cppfront) -- all end up as
PTX handed to the same backend. ptxas builds the ELF container our code is
spliced into (README.md "How it works"); see openassembler/build.py.

symbols.name: cmd_run
symbols.doc:
Run the cubins in OUTDIR (from a previous `compile`) on a real GPU, ours and
ptxas's reference build side by side on identical inputs; bit-exact comparison
and timing per kernel. See openassembler/runner.py for the auto-harness and the
--spec format.

symbols.name: cmd_cnr
symbols.doc:
compile SRC into --out-dir, then run every kernel that compiled (`run`). Kernels
that failed to compile are reported and not run; nonzero exit if anything failed.

symbols.name: cmd_verify
symbols.doc:
Run an already-built cubin's SASS through the emulator and compare
against the PTX reference interpreter on random inputs (same check
compile_check.py and bench_build.py use before trusting a build). Only
for kernels matching the probe corpus's fixed (out, in, k, kf) ABI --
for your own kernel's own signature, use `compile --verify`, which picks
this or the generic checker (openassembler.verify) automatically.

symbols.name: cmd_check
symbols.doc:
Compile the full probe corpus, validate with nvdisasm, check semantics
against the PTX interpreter. Needs the probe corpus (tools/build_corpus.py)
and ptxas. Wraps tools/compile_check.py.

symbols.name: cmd_corpus
symbols.doc:
Build the probe corpus (541 PTX probes -> ptxas -> cubin + SASS) under
corpus/<arch>/. Needed once before `check`, `gpu run`, or the offline
A100-replay tests; needs the CUDA toolkit. Wraps tools/build_corpus.py.

symbols.name: cmd_bench
symbols.doc:
Build the microbenchmark cubins at every optimization level
(safe/mined/sched/opt), each checked in the emulator first. Wraps
tools/bench_build.py. Pair with `openassembler gpu run` to time them.

symbols.name: cmd_fastmm
symbols.doc:
Fast matrix multiplication: build Strassen/AlphaTensor-scheme GEMM
kernels with our compiler (tools/fastmm_build.py), or run a plan on a GPU
(tools/fastmm_run.py, Modal only -- for SSH/local use `gpu run` on the
cubins fastmm build produces).

symbols.name: cmd_gpu
symbols.doc:
Run probe or built cubins on a real GPU and compare against the
emulator / PTX spec. Default backend is any machine you can SSH into with
an NVIDIA driver (no CUDA toolkit needed there) -- this is the
reproduction path anyone without a cloud GPU account can use. `--backend
modal` is what produced the numbers recorded in corpus/ for this repo.

symbols.name: cmd_status
symbols.doc: Print the headline, reproducible numbers from docs/STATUS.md.

symbols.name: dispatch
symbols.doc:
Run a parsed command. Ctrl-C anywhere: remove half-written outputs (temp files
of writes in flight; finished files are renamed into place atomically), print one
line, exit 130 -- the shell convention for SIGINT.

openassembler/container/cubin.py.doc:
Write a kernel's code into a cubin built by ptxas for the same PTX signature.

We reuse ptxas's ELF skeleton (symbols, .nv.constant0, .nv.info, relocations) and
replace `.text.<kernel>`, then fix every place that describes the code:
  * .text.<k> sh_info bits 24..31  register count (the driver allocates from this;
    a stale value makes the kernel fault with CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION)
  * .nv.info  EIATTR_REGCOUNT      register count
  * .nv.info.<k> EXIT_INSTR_OFFSETS
  * the function symbol's size     (nvdisasm rejects a mismatch)

symbols.name: required_regcount
symbols.doc:
Register count to declare for code that touches the given SASS texts.

Measured on A100 (corpus/sm_80/gpu_a100_40gb_bisect5.json, 77 variants):
an instruction writing Rd faults with CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION unless
the declared count >= Rd + 3 (the top two slots are reserved), with no
fault for any Rd <= 13 at the minimum count of 16 used by ptxas. Wide
operands (.64 = 2, .128 = 4 registers) count their last register.

openassembler/container/elf.py.doc:
Minimal ELF64 reader/writer for CUDA cubins (EM_CUDA = 190).

Design goal: `Elf.parse(b).serialize() == b` for ptxas output, so we can edit
sections (e.g. replace .text.<kernel>) and write a valid cubin. We keep the
original file layout (offsets, padding, program headers) and only re-layout when
a section's size changes.

symbols.name: replace_data
symbols.doc:
Replace a section's bytes. If the size changes, later sections move.
For `.text.<k>`, the function symbol of the same name gets the new size.

symbols.name: _fix_phdrs
symbols.doc:
Program headers on cubins describe the PT_PHDR and PT_LOAD of code/data
sections. Recompute each segment's extent from the sections it covers.

openassembler/container/nvinfo.py.doc:
`.nv.info` / `.nv.info.<kernel>` attribute records.

Every record starts with a 4-byte header: format byte, attribute byte, u16 field.
  0x01 EIFMT_NVAL  u16 unused (0)
  0x02 EIFMT_BVAL  u16 holds the byte value
  0x03 EIFMT_HVAL  u16 holds the value
  0x04 EIFMT_SVAL  u16 = payload size, followed by `size` bytes
Measured on smoke.cubin ("01 35 00 00", "03 19 18 00" = CBANK_PARAM_SIZE 0x18,
"03 1b ff 00" = MAXREG_COUNT 0xff), round-trip-checked on the whole corpus.

openassembler/cppfront.py.doc:
CUDA C/C++ -> PTX, via nvcc's own frontend and NVVM optimizer (--ptx).

Unlike the SASS side of this project, we don't reverse-engineer C++ parsing
or NVVM's optimizer -- nvcc is already vendored as a black-box *oracle*
(env/cuda.sh, used everywhere else in this repo to check our own work), and
turning C++ into PTX is squarely what it's for. What we replace is
everything downstream of PTX: our own backend (openassembler.backend.ra) takes
nvcc's PTX and generates the SASS itself, same as for hand-written PTX or
openassembler.pyfront's output. See README.md "How it works" -- this is the same
"reuse the container, replace the code generator" split, just one level
earlier in the pipeline.

Kernels should be `extern "C" __global__ void name(...)` so nvcc doesn't
C++-name-mangle them -- otherwise --entry has to match the mangled symbol,
which this module does not attempt to demangle for you.

symbols.name: compile_to_ptx_module
symbols.doc:
Run `nvcc --ptx` on a .cu/.cuh/.cpp/.cc/.cxx file; return (ptx_text, every
__global__ entry in it). The file is compiled as CUDA (`-x cu`) whatever its
extension: nvcc treats .cpp as host-only C++ (where __global__ is undefined)
and refuses .cuh outright, but a repo's kernels live in all of these.
include_dirs become -I flags (the file's own directory is always first, so
`#include "local.h"` works even when the source is staged, see below);
extra_flags are passed to nvcc verbatim (-D..., -std=c++17, ...).
On macOS nvcc runs in the colima VM, which only mounts $HOME; a source outside
it is compiled from a scratch copy, and its #includes must then be reachable
from under $HOME too. Raises CppFrontendError with nvcc's own message on a
compile error, or if nvcc produced no kernels. The intermediate .ptx goes to
a scratch file and is removed -- nothing is written next to your source.

symbols.name: compile_to_ptx
symbols.doc:
Single-kernel form of compile_to_ptx_module: (ptx_text, kernel_name), where
`entry` picks the kernel when the file has several.

openassembler/emu/__init__.py.doc:
SASS emulator: executes nvdisasm-text programs for one CTA, warp by warp.

Validated against ptxas output first (emulator(ptxas SASS) == PTX interpreter),
then used to check our own compiler's SASS.

openassembler/emu/fp.py.doc:
Exact IEEE-754 binary32/binary64 arithmetic for the emulator.

Finite values become exact Fractions, the operation is done exactly, and the
result is rounded once with the requested mode. That gives correctly rounded
FADD/FMUL/FFMA/I2F/F2F under RN/RZ/RM/RP, with flush-to-zero (FTZ) as an option.

Hardware-approximate ops (MUFU) are modeled as correctly rounded, marked
HYPOTHESIS: real MUFU.RCP etc. have ~1 ulp error, so emulated results can
legitimately differ from a GPU. Integer division sequences built on MUFU.RCP
are exact by construction, which the differential harness checks.

symbols.name: Val
symbols.doc: Decoded float: exactly one of nan / inf / finite (with sign for zero).

symbols.name: _round_int
symbols.doc: Round a non-negative rational to an integer under mode (for |value|).

symbols.name: encode
symbols.doc:
NaN results (measured on A100, corpus/sm_80/gpu_a100_40gb.json):
  f32 arithmetic       -> canonical 0x7fffffff
  f64 arithmetic       -> the input NaN, payload and sign kept, quieted
  F2F (keep_nan=True)  -> sign kept, payload shifted to the new width, quieted
A NaN created from non-NaN inputs (inf - inf) in f64 is still a HYPOTHESIS.

symbols.name: cmp
symbols.doc: -1/0/1, or None if unordered.

symbols.name: to_int
symbols.doc:
F2I: round then saturate. NaN (PTX ISA 9.x cvt, confirmed on A100):
0 if the source is not f64 and the destination is not 64-bit, else 1 << (bits - 1).

openassembler/emu/machine.py.doc:
Machine state and execution loop for one CTA.

Model: every thread has its own PC (Volta+ independent thread scheduling).
Each warp repeatedly picks the lowest PC among its live threads and executes
that instruction for all threads sitting at it. For structured code this
reconverges exactly where BSSY/BSYNC would, so convergence barriers are no-ops.
Warp collectives (SHFL, VOTE, ...) see the lanes executing together.

symbols.name: Memory
symbols.doc: Sparse byte-addressed little-endian memory.

symbols.name: rd
symbols.doc: Read an integer source operand (no neg/not applied).

symbols.name: src
symbols.doc: 32-bit integer source with '-' (2's complement) and '~' applied.

symbols.name: addr
symbols.doc:
`wide` overrides the operand's .64 marker: nvdisasm prints ATOMG.E's address
as [R2] although .E (extended) means a 64-bit register pair.

symbols.name: run
symbols.doc:
Warps run one at a time until they finish or reach a CTA barrier. With several
warps, BAR.SYNC is cooperative: a warp stops at the barrier, and when every live
warp is waiting, all of them pass it together.

openassembler/emu/operands.py.doc: Parse nvdisasm operand text into typed operands.

symbols.name: _f32_text_to_bits
symbols.doc:
nvdisasm's decimal text for a float immediate, as its raw 32 bits.
f32-range values (FADD/FSETP/FFMA/...) round-trip through struct directly;
a double-precision instruction's immediate (DMUL/DSETP/...) can exceed
f32's range, and only its high 32 bits sit in a 32-bit immediate slot --
see ops.py's _fsel note on FSEL selecting raw f64 high words.

symbols.name: split_operands
symbols.doc: Split on top-level commas (none occur inside [] in practice, but be safe).

symbols.name: int32
symbols.doc:
The raw 32 bits nvdisasm's text represents. Most immediates are
plain decimal/hex integers; FSETP/FADD/etc. print their immediate as
a decimal float in scientific notation (e.g. "1.175494350822287508e-38")
or +INF/-INF/NAN/+QNAN -- those parse as the IEEE-754 f32 bit pattern
of that value, which is what actually sits in the word's immediate
field for a float-typed instruction.

symbols.name: f32bits
symbols.doc:
The text read as a FLOAT, whatever it looks like: nvdisasm prints some float
immediates as plain integers ("FMUL R0, R1, 4096" means 4096.0, bits 0x45800000),
which int32() would take as the raw bits 0x1000. Text that is explicitly hex
("0x40000000", which is how our own compiler writes a float constant) IS the raw bits.

symbols.name: lut3
symbols.doc:
LOP3 truth table: bit i of `lut` is the output for (a,b,c) = bits of i (a = MSB).
Equivalent to NAK's LogicOp3::eval; lut 0xF0 = a, 0xCC = b, 0xAA = c.

symbols.name: split_pred_dsts
symbols.doc: Pop leading predicate *destinations* that follow the register dst.

symbols.name: h2_operands
symbols.doc:
Read packed-half sources. A register (optionally .H0_H0 / .H1_H1) gives
(lo, hi); a pair of immediates "hi, lo" gives one source. Returns [(lo, hi), ...].

symbols.name: fsrc
symbols.doc: Float source: immediates are decimal text, others are raw bits; then |x| and -x.

symbols.name: float_atomic
symbols.doc: ATOM*.ADD.F32.FTZ.RN / ADD.F64.RN: IEEE add, round-to-nearest (f32 flushes subnormals).

symbols.name: _inv_sqrt
symbols.doc:
floor(1/sqrt(q)) with >= 120 significant bits, for any magnitude (exact
integer square root). The old fixed-point 2^-200 version returned 0 for
q > 2^400, which the A100 replay of sqrt.rn.f64 exposed.

openassembler/emu/probe.py.doc:
Run one probe kernel (tools/ptx_probes.py ABI) on the SASS emulator.

Probe ABI: params (out: u64, in: u64, k: u32, kf: f32) at c[0x0][param_base..+24].
Each thread t reads 16 bytes at in + 16*t and writes 8 bytes at out + 16*t.

symbols.name: cubin_consts
symbols.doc:
Constant banks other than bank 0 that ptxas initialized in the cubin
(.nv.constant2.<k>: jump tables for BRX; .nv.constant3: user .const data).

symbols.name: run_probe
symbols.doc: inputs[t] = 4 x u32 for thread t; returns (out_lo, out_hi) per thread.

openassembler/emu/program.py.doc: Load an `nvdisasm -hex -c` listing into executable instructions.

symbols.name: load_listing
symbols.doc:
Parse one kernel's code section. Labels (incl. internal subroutines in the
same section) map to the address of the next instruction.

openassembler/emu/tensor.py.doc:
Warp-level matrix ops: HMMA / IMMA / DMMA, LDSM, LDGSTS.

Fragment layouts are the PTX ISA's (9.7.16.5.x, "Matrix Fragments for mma.mMnNkK").
With groupID = lane >> 2 and tig = lane % 4:

  m16n8k16 f16/bf16  A[16x16]: a_i  row = g (+8 if i in {2,3,6,7})  col = 2*tig + (i&1) (+8 if i >= 4)
                     B[16x8]:  b_i  k = 2*tig + (i&1) (+8 if i >= 2)  n = g
  m16n8k8  tf32      A[16x8]:  a_i  row = g (+8 if i odd)            col = tig (+4 if i >= 2)
                     B[8x8]:   b_i  k = tig (+4 if i == 1)            n = g
  m16n8k32 s8/u8     A[16x32]: a_i  row = g (+8 if i in 4..7 or 12..15)  col = 4*tig + (i&3) (+16 if i >= 8)
                     B[32x8]:  b_i  k = 4*tig + (i&3) (+16 if i >= 4)    n = g
  m8n8k4   f64       A[8x4]:   row = g, col = tig;  B[4x8]: k = tig, n = g
  C/D (all m16n8):   c_i  row = g (+8 if i >= 2)  col = 2*tig + (i&1)
  C/D (m8n8k4 f64):  c_i  row = g, col = 2*tig + i

Accumulation numerics are a *model* (MMA_MODEL below) whose parameters are fitted
to A100 outputs by tools/fit_mma.py; the defaults are the fitted values.

symbols.name: _exp2
symbols.doc: floor(log2(q)) for q > 0.

symbols.name: aligned_sum
dot_f32
symbols.doc: D = sum(a*b for a, b in pairs) + c as f32 bits, using the fitted model.

symbols.name: ldsm
symbols.doc:
LDSM.16.{M88,MT88}.{1,2,4} Rd, [Ra+off]  (PTX ldmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.xN[.trans].b16).
Matrix j's 8 row addresses come from lanes 8j..8j+7. Each lane receives, for every
matrix j, one 32-bit register: elements (row = lane>>2, col = 2*(lane&3) + {0,1});
with .trans (MT88) the matrix is transposed first.

symbols.name: ldgsts
symbols.doc:
LDGSTS.E[.BYPASS][.64|.128] [Rs], [Rg.64]: global -> shared copy. Modeled as
synchronous (it completes before LDGDEPBAR/DEPBAR, which are no-ops here).

openassembler/fastmm/__init__.py.doc: Fast (sub-cubic) matrix multiplication schemes: AlphaTensor factorizations -> SASS.

openassembler/fastmm/factors.py.doc:
Load and verify bilinear matrix-multiplication schemes (rank-R tensor decompositions).

A scheme for <n, m, p> (A: n x m, B: m x p, C = A B: n x p) is three integer/rational
matrices u [n*m, R], v [m*p, R], w [n*p, R]:

    M_r = (sum_{ij} u[i*m+j, r] A_ij) * (sum_{jk} v[j*p+k, r] B_jk)        r = 0..R-1
    C_ik = sum_r w[?, r] M_r

AlphaTensor stores w for the *transposed* product (index k*n+i, see
alphatensor/benchmarking/utils.py: "factors[2] = factors[2].transpose(1, 0, 2)").
verify() checks the exact tensor identity over the rationals, and load() normalizes w to
row-major C (index i*p+k).

Sources (third_party/alphatensor, fetched from github.com/google-deepmind/alphatensor):
  algorithms/factorizations_r.npz        93 schemes over the reals (int / dyadic coefs)
  benchmarking/factorizations.py         the V100-tuned 4x4x4 rank-49 scheme, Strassen^2
The .npz holds pickled numpy object arrays; tools/fastmm_import.py converts it once into
specs/fastmm/schemes.json.gz (sparse, stdlib-readable).

symbols.name: strassen
symbols.doc: Strassen 1969, <2,2,2> rank 7, written in this module's convention.

symbols.name: verify
symbols.doc: Exact check of sum_r u[a,r] v[b,r] w[c,r] == T[a,b,c] for every (a,b,c).

symbols.name: additions
symbols.doc:
Nonzeros-minus-one per product for the A sums, B sums, and C accumulation:
the scalar/block additions a direct (no CSE) evaluation needs.

openassembler/fastmm/kernels.py.doc:
PTX generators for the kernels a block fast-matmul plan launches.

sgemm   C = A B  (fp32, row-major, leading dimensions in elements). One CTA computes a
        64 x 64 tile of C with 256 threads; each thread a 4 x 4 sub-tile. K is consumed
        8 at a time through shared memory (A stored transposed: As[k][m]); the next
        k-tile is loaded from global memory into registers while the current one is
        multiplied. Requires M % 64 == N % 64 == 0, K % 8 == 0, lda/ldb/ldc % 4 == 0.
        Grid: (N/64, M/64).

lincomb out = sum_j c_j * in_j over a rows x cols block (each operand a strided view).
        One thread handles 4 consecutive floats. Grid: (ceil(cols/1024), rows), 256
        threads; requires cols % 4 == 0 and 16-byte aligned views.

Both are plain PTX so that the same source can be compiled by ptxas and by our
compiler (openassembler.backend.ra), which is how they are compared.

symbols.name: _gload
symbols.doc: Load the k-tile starting at column k (A) / row k (B, kb = k*ldb) into %g0..%g3.

symbols.name: sgemm128
symbols.doc:
128 x 128 C tile per CTA, 256 threads, 8 x 8 outputs per thread (rows ty*4+{0..3},
64+ty*4+{0..3}; same split for columns, so LDS.128 reads are conflict-free), BK = 8,
double-buffered shared memory (one barrier per k-tile), next tile prefetched into
registers with 128-bit global loads. Requires M, N % 128 == 0, K % 8 == 0,
lda/ldb/ldc % 4 == 0 and 16-byte aligned views. Grid (N/128, M/128).

symbols.name: fgemm
symbols.doc:
Fused rank-1 step of a bilinear scheme, on the sgemm128 tiling:

    for each output o:  C_o += w_o * (sum_s u_s A_s) (sum_t v_t B_t)

The A/B linear combinations are formed in registers while a k-tile is loaded
(ka / kb 128-bit global loads per thread instead of one), and the epilogue does a
read-modify-write of every C_o (kc of them), so no temporaries S_r, T_r, M_r and no
separate add kernels exist. All A_s share lda, all B_t ldb, all C_o ldc. Launches of
one plan run in stream order, so the read-modify-writes of different steps on the
same C block cannot race. C must be zeroed before the first step.

symbols.name: _gload_comb
symbols.doc: %g0..3 = sum_s cA_s * A_s[row, k + r7 .. +3];  %g4..7 = sum_t cB_t * B_t[k + r8, cols].

openassembler/fastmm/plan.py.doc:
Turn a bilinear scheme into a GPU launch plan (one level of block recursion).

C (N x N) = A B with A, B split into n x m and m x p grids of blocks of size bs:

  for r in 0..R-1:
      S_r = sum_ij u[ij, r] A_ij             lincomb kernel   (skipped if one term with coef 1)
      T_r = sum_jk v[jk, r] B_jk             lincomb kernel   (same)
      M_r = S_r T_r                          sgemm kernel on bs x bs blocks
  C_ik  = sum_r w[ik, r] M_r                 lincomb kernel, chunked to <= MAXIN inputs

Views are (buffer, element offset, leading dimension), so single-term operands read A/B/C
directly. Coefficients are exact in f32 (integers / dyadic fractions). The naive scheme
naive(n, m, p) gives the same plan structure with R = n m p and no linear combinations,
which is the fair "same kernels, cubic" baseline; one big sgemm launch is the other.

symbols.name: _lincomb
symbols.doc: out = sum c * in (or out += ... if accumulate) over a rows x cols view.

symbols.name: cublas
symbols.doc: Reference: one cublasSgemm (FP32 CUDA cores, default math mode, no TF32).

symbols.name: build
symbols.doc: One recursion level of scheme s on N x N matrices (N divisible by 64 n, 64 m, 64 p).

symbols.name: build_fused
symbols.doc:
Like build(), but each rank-1 step whose A, B and C term counts are <= FUSE_MAX is
one fgemm launch (openassembler.fastmm.kernels.fgemm): the linear combinations happen while
tiles are loaded and C_o += w_o M_r in the epilogue. Other steps use the unfused path
(lincomb -> sgemm128 -> accumulate). C is zeroed first.

openassembler/frontend.py.doc:
Turns any supported source file into PTX for the backend, so
openassembler.backend.ra always starts from PTX text regardless of whether the
source was already PTX, a Python kernel (openassembler.pyfront), or CUDA C/C++
(openassembler.cppfront, which shells out to nvcc once -- see its docstring for
why that's not "cheating" the same way ptxas's code generation would be).

to_ptx_module() is what `openassembler compile` uses: one source file -> one PTX
module holding ALL of its kernels (they end up in one cubin). to_ptx() is the
older single-kernel form, kept for callers that want exactly one kernel.

symbols.name: _merge_ptx
symbols.doc:
Several single-kernel PTX modules (pyfront emits one per @kernel) -> one module:
keep the first module's .version/.target/.address_size header, drop the repeats.

symbols.name: _python_module
symbols.doc: Statically compile all supported @kernel definitions; never import user code.

symbols.name: to_ptx_module
symbols.doc:
(ptx_text, kernel names in source order, notes). Raises FrontendError for an
unsupported extension; the frontends' own errors (pyfront.NotSupported,
cppfront.CppFrontendError) propagate unchanged for the caller to report.

symbols.name: to_ptx
symbols.doc:
Returns (ptx_text, kernel_name). `entry` selects which kernel/function
to compile when the source has more than one; for .ptx with exactly one
kernel it's optional, same as before this function existed.

openassembler/gpu/__init__.py.doc: Run cubins on real GPUs: ctypes driver-API loader + transport-independent batch runner.

openassembler/gpu/batch.py.doc:
Transport-independent GPU batch runner (stdlib only).

    python -m openassembler.gpu.batch jobs.pkl results.pkl [--job-timeout 20] [--budget 600]

Runs on the GPU host. Jobs are processed in chunks by a worker *subprocess*; if
a kernel faults (poisoned context) or hangs, the worker is killed, that job is
recorded as an error, and a fresh worker resumes with the next job. A global
`--budget` (seconds) stops the whole batch early so a remote host never runs
away with billing; unfinished jobs are reported as "skipped-budget".

The same entry point is used by every transport: Modal (tools/gpu_modal.py),
SSH (tools/gpu_run.py --ssh host), or a local GPU (tools/gpu_run.py --local).

symbols.name: worker
symbols.doc: Runs jobs[start:] in this process, appending results to out_path as it goes.

openassembler/gpu/cuda_driver.py.doc:
Load and run cubins with the CUDA *driver* API via ctypes on libcuda.so.

Stdlib only, so it runs on any Linux host with an NVIDIA driver: Modal containers
(libcuda is mounted, no toolkit needed), an SSH box, or a local workstation.

Robustness:
  * every driver call is checked; error names come from cuGetErrorName
  * a kernel fault poisons the CUDA context, so callers that batch many cubins
    should run each in its own process (see openassembler.gpu.batch)
  * memory beyond the probe slot is guarded: we allocate padding and fill it
    with a canary to detect out-of-bounds writes

symbols.name: run_probe_job
symbols.doc:
job: {kname, cubin, trials: [(inputs[32][4], k, kf)]} -> {out, attrs, oob}.
Caller owns the context.

symbols.name: time_probe_job
symbols.doc:
Timing mode: launch the probe kernel with `grid` blocks x 32 threads, `reps`
times after `warmup` launches; report per-launch GPU time (cuEvent) statistics.
Inputs come from trial 0. Correctness is checked separately (run_probe_job), since
every block writes the same per-thread output slots under the probe ABI.

symbols.name: rand_f32
symbols.doc:
Deterministic uniform(-1, 1) f32 data, identical on the host and in the container
(random.Random is specified to be reproducible across platforms). Cached.

symbols.name: run_plan_job
symbols.doc:
job = {
    "modules": {name: cubin bytes},
    "buffers": {name: size_bytes},
    "init":    {buffer: bytes}               host data copied in once
    "init_rand": {buffer: (seed, count)}     or generated with rand_f32 (no upload)
    "steps":   [(module, kernel, grid, block, smem, [arg, ...]), ...]
               arg: ("buf", name, byte_offset) | ("u32", v) | ("f32bits", v) | ("u64", v)
    "outputs": {buffer: [(offset, nbytes)]}  read back after one run
    "reps", "warmup": timing of the whole step list (cuEvents around it)
}
Stdlib only. Returns {"out": {buf: bytes}, "time_ms": {...}, "attrs": {...}}.

symbols.name: Cublas
symbols.doc:
Minimal cuBLAS (libcublas.so.*, e.g. from pip nvidia-cublas-cu12) for a reference
SGEMM in plans. Row-major C = A B is computed as column-major C^T = B^T A^T.

symbols.name: func_attrs
symbols.doc: Driver-reported kernel resources (CU_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_*): checks our .nv.info.

symbols.name: launch
symbols.doc: args: list of ctypes scalars. Returns kernel time in ms if time_it.

openassembler/gpu/modal_app.py.doc:
Generic Modal app for `openassembler run --backend modal` (and `cnr`): runs a jobs
pickle (openassembler.gpu.cuda_driver.run_plan_job format, built by
openassembler.runner) on one Modal GPU container and writes the results pickle.

    modal run openassembler/gpu/modal_app.py --jobs jobs.pkl --out res.pkl         [--gpu A100-40GB] [--budget 300] [--job-timeout 60]

openassembler invokes this through the `modal` CLI as a subprocess, so the modal
package only has to be installed in whatever Python env provides `modal` (it is
not a dependency of openassembler). Setup once: pip install modal && modal setup.

Billing safety (Modal bills a container from start to exit), same layers as
tools/gpu_modal.py:
  * `modal run` is an ephemeral app: it stops when this local process exits. If the
    local process is killed hard, `modal app list` / `modal app stop <id>`.
  * per-job watchdog in openassembler.gpu.batch (kills a hung kernel's worker), the
    global --budget inside the container, and Modal's own function timeout
    (hard kill) = budget + 60 s; max_containers=1, retries=0.
  * one container runs the whole batch: one cold start, then jobs back to back.
The container gets only openassembler/__init__.py + openassembler/gpu/ (stdlib-only)
and the jobs pickle; the comparison happens locally (openassembler.runner).

openassembler/isa/encode.py.doc:
Template encoder: SASS text -> 128-bit word, by patching a known word.

Strategy (M3 "encoder patches templates"): pick a corpus word with the same
mnemonic+modifiers and the same operand *kinds*, then rewrite only fields whose
positions are verified (docs/findings-sm80-encoding.md):
  guard 12..15, Rd 16..23, Ra 24..31, Rb 32..39 | imm32 32..63 | cbank 38..58, Rc 64..71,
  and the control bits 105..125.
Operand-slot -> field mapping is *learned* per template group from the corpus:
for each operand position we find which field holds its value in every example.
Anything not learnable is refused (EncodeError) rather than guessed.

symbols.name: _load_json_tolerant
symbols.doc:
bitflip.json may have tools/bitflip.py's text report in front of it when the
tool's stdout was redirected into the spec file; parse from the first '{' line.

symbols.name: _disambiguate
symbols.doc:
Break ties using the bit-flip map (specs/<arch>/bitflip.json): keep fields whose
bits were observed to change operand `pos` for this opcode/form.

symbols.name: field_probe
symbols.doc:
Flip every bit of `word` in the operand regions and record which operand text
changed (one nvdisasm batch). -> {bit: "opN"}. Used to learn the field map of a
synthesized (single-example) template instead of guessing canonical positions.

The answer depends only on (word, arch), so it's cached in specs/sm_80/
synth_fieldmaps.json. Without the cache, building an Encoder re-ran this ~60
times through nvdisasm at every start (a minute on macOS, where nvdisasm runs
in a VM) and needed the NVIDIA toolkit just to load. With it, loading is
instant and offline; a word that isn't cached yet is probed once and added.

symbols.name: synthesize
symbols.doc:
For texts with no template, try known words of the same opcode with every
combination of 1-2 flipped bits in the modifier region (72..90) and the form bits
(9..11), disassemble the candidates in one nvdisasm batch, and adopt any word whose
text has exactly the wanted key. Accepted words are cached in specs/<arch>/
synth_templates.json and loaded by Encoder() like corpus words.
Returns the number of new templates.

symbols.name: minimize
symbols.doc:
Canonicalize bits that nvdisasm does not print. A seed word's leftover bits can sit
in fields the hardware reads: a synthesized ISETP kept 0xad of an old immediate in bits
32..39 and made every loop on the A100 run one extra iteration. Clearing such bits is
wrong too (bits 68..70 of ISETP are a hidden PT = 7). So each bit whose flip leaves the
text unchanged is set to the majority value among `peers` (corpus words with the same
opcode and form bits), when that majority still disassembles identically.

symbols.name: _learn
symbols.doc:
canonical=True (synthesized, single-example templates): an operand slot whose
field is ambiguous falls back to the canonical Volta+ field for its position
(first R -> rd 16..23, then ra 24..31, rb 32..39, rc 64..71; cbank 38..58).
Callers must verify such words with nvdisasm (tools/compile_check.py does).

symbols.name: encode_branch
symbols.doc:
BRA/BSSY/CALL.REL with a resolved target address. Offset = target - (addr + 16),
signed; BRA/CALL hold it at bits 34..81 in units of 4 bytes, BSSY at 34..63
(bitflip map, specs/sm_80/bitflip.json).

Generic fields of a Volta+ (sm_70..sm_120) 128-bit SASS instruction word.

These are the fields shared by (almost) every instruction. Per-opcode fields
(modifiers, operand kinds) come from specs/<arch>/*.json, discovered by tools/.
Bit positions are verified on real sm_80 words; see tests/test_word.py.

symbols.name: Control

symbols.name: control_valid

openassembler/opt/__init__.py.doc: Middle-end rewrites (idioms, strength reduction), each proved with z3.

openassembler/opt/divconst.py.doc:
Integer division / remainder by a constant -> multiply-high sequences.

Algorithms: Granlund & Montgomery (1994) / Hacker's Delight ch. 10, written here
as straight-line programs over a tiny SASS-like IR so the same object can be
(1) emitted as SASS, (2) emulated, and (3) proved equal to x / d with z3.

IR ops (32-bit unless noted):
  ("mulhi_u", dst, a, imm)       dst = (a * imm) >> 32        -> IMAD.HI.U32
  ("mulhi_s", dst, a, imm)       dst = (sext(a) * sext(imm)) >> 32   -> IMAD.HI
  ("shr_u", dst, a, k)           logical shift                 -> SHF.R.U32.HI
  ("shr_s", dst, a, k)           arithmetic shift              -> SHF.R.S32.HI
  ("sub", dst, a, b) / ("add", dst, a, b)                      -> IADD3
  ("lea_hi_sign", dst, a, b)     dst = a + (b >>> 31)          -> LEA.HI
  ("mad", dst, q, imm, x)        dst = q * imm + x             -> IMAD
  ("mov", dst, a)
Operand: register name (str) or int immediate.

symbols.name: sdiv
symbols.doc: Signed division (truncating) by a positive constant 2 <= d < 2^31.

symbols.name: with_rem
symbols.doc: Append r = x - q*d (one IMAD with -d).

symbols.name: prove
symbols.doc:
Return 'proved', 'refuted: x=...' or 'unknown'.

Division-free specification (SAT-friendly; avoids bit-blasting a divider):
  unsigned: q*d <= x < (q+1)*d                       (64-bit, no overflow)
  signed:   x >= 0: q*d <= x < (q+1)*d ;  x < 0: (q-1)*d < x <= q*d
For `rem`, the sequence is <div prefix> ; r = q*(-d) + x. We prove the prefix
computes the true quotient q; then r = x - q*d holds by construction, and
0 <= |r| < d means no 32-bit wraparound changes it.

symbols.name: to_sass
symbols.doc: Render as SASS text (registers R2.. allocated in order).

openassembler/oracle.py.doc:
Black-box oracle: NVIDIA's ptxas/nvdisasm run through env/cuda.sh.

The oracle turns raw 128-bit words into nvdisasm's text (or None when nvdisasm
rejects the encoding), and compiles PTX into cubins. Everything else in openassembler
is validated against it.

Word convention: a Volta+ instruction is one Python int `w = lo | (hi << 64)`,
stored little-endian as two qwords (lo first), exactly as in a cubin .text.

Run an NVIDIA tool from the project root: directly on Linux, inside the
colima VM on macOS (both handled by env/cuda.sh).

colima VM isn't running. Cached per process; used by tests to skip rather than

VM that only mounts $HOME, so a path outside $HOME can't be seen and raises

symbols.doc:
`nvdisasm -hex -c` output for a cubin: the .sass text, two lines per

openassembler/project.py.doc:
Project layout for `openassembler compile` / `run` / `cnr`: which files in a
source tree are kernels, where their outputs go, and the manifest that ties the
two together.

Output folder (default ./output, `--out-dir DIR`):

    output/cubin/<name>.cubin            our SASS, in a ptxas-built ELF container (loadable by the driver)
    output/sass/<name>.sass              nvdisasm's listing of exactly that cubin
    output/manifest.json                 what was compiled, from what, by whom (schema below)
    output/.build/ptx/<name>.ptx         the PTX that was compiled (frontend output for .py/.cu)
    output/.build/reference/<name>.cubin ptxas -O3 on the same PTX: `run`'s correctness/speed reference
    output/run.json                      the last `run`/`cnr` report (written by openassembler.runner)

<name> is the source's stem for a single file (or `-o NAME`); for a directory it
is the source's path relative to the root with the extension replaced
(kernels/gemm.cu -> cubin/kernels/gemm.cubin), keeping the full filename when two
sources in one directory share a stem (a.cu + a.py -> a.cu.cubin, a.py.cubin).

manifest.json schema (version 1; `openassembler run` reads nothing else):

    {"openassembler": "0.2.0",              version that wrote it (run warns on a mismatch)
     "arch": "sm_80", "opt_level": "opt",
     "root": "/abs/path",                   SRC itself (a directory) or a single SRC's directory
     "entries": [{
        "source": "kernels/gemm.cu",        relative to root when under it, else absolute
        "source_sha256": "...",             run warns "out of date" when the file changed
        "language": "ptx" | "python" | "cuda",
        "cubin": "cubin/kernels/gemm.cubin",            all four paths relative to the output folder
        "sass": "sass/kernels/gemm.sass" | null,        (null with --no-sass)
        "ptx": ".build/ptx/kernels/gemm.ptx",
        "reference": ".build/reference/kernels/gemm.cubin",
        "kernels": [{"name": "gemm", "params": [["u64", "a"], ["u32", "n"], ...],
                     "compiled_by": "openassembler" | "ptxas-fallback",
                     "instructions": 42, "registers": 24,
                     "verify": "ok" | "failed" | "not-run" | "not-verified",
                     "note": "...",                       optional: why it fell back / wasn't verified
                     "source_params": ["a", "b", "n"]}],  optional: CUDA C names of params (nvcc's
                                                          PTX calls them <kernel>_param_<i>)
        "failed": [{"name": "k2", "error": "..."}]}]}   kernels left out of this cubin (optional)

Rules the compile command keeps (see openassembler.build): an entry's outputs are
exactly the files listed in it; a single-file compile replaces only the entry with
the same cubin path; outputs of entries whose source no longer exists are deleted,
and nothing outside the output folder or not listed in the previous manifest is
ever deleted. Every file is written to a temp name and renamed into place, so an
interrupted compile (Ctrl-C) never leaves a half-written output.

openassembler/ptx/__init__.py.doc:
PTX frontend: parser and reference interpreter.

The interpreter is the semantic reference for the differential harness:
emulator(ptxas SASS) must equal interpreter(PTX) on the same inputs.
It is written from the PTX ISA spec, independently of the SASS emulator.

openassembler/ptx/interp.py.doc:
Reference PTX interpreter (one CTA, lock-step warps).

Semantics come from the PTX ISA spec, not from SASS. Values are stored as raw
bits per register; each instruction's type suffix says how to read them.
Undefined-by-spec results (div/rem by zero, shift >= width handled per spec)
follow the spec where it defines them and raise `Undefined` where it doesn't,
so the harness can skip those lanes instead of encoding ptxas's choice as truth.

Execution model: a warp runs in lock-step with an active mask. Divergent
branches are handled by a reconvergence stack (immediate post-dominator =
the lowest pending pc, valid for the reducible, forward-structured code in our
probes); collectives see the active lanes.

CTA barriers (bar.sync / barrier.sync / bar.arrive / bar.red, any warp count)
are cooperative, mirroring the SASS emulator's Machine.run: each warp runs
until all its lanes have exited or are parked at a barrier; a barrier
completes when its expected arrivals are in -- for the full-CTA form, every
non-exited thread of the CTA (sm_70+ per-thread semantics: exited threads
count as arrived, which is what makes `if (i >= n) return; ... __syncthreads()`
work) -- and its waiters then resume. See Interp._bar_arrive for the exact
rules and for what is rejected instead of guessed.

symbols.name: Undefined
symbols.doc: Result is undefined by the PTX spec (e.g. integer division by zero).

symbols.name: _Barrier
symbols.doc: One of the CTA's 16 named barriers, between two completions.

symbols.name: _bar_arrive
symbols.doc:
Threads `lanes` (one warp, same pc) execute bar/barrier .sync/.arrive/.red.

Rules (PTX ISA "bar, barrier", sm_70+ per-thread semantics), and where we
refuse instead of guessing:
  * guard-false threads don't execute it and just move on;
  * full-CTA form (no thread count): completes when every non-exited
    thread of the CTA has arrived; exited threads count as arrived;
  * counted form (bar.sync b, n / bar.arrive b, n): the spec counts
    arrivals in warp-size units, so a counted arrival must come from a
    whole, non-exited, converged warp -- anything else is NotModeled, as
    is a count that isn't a positive multiple of 32 or exceeds the CTA;
  * .aligned (all bar.* forms, barrier.*.aligned): every thread of a warp
    must execute the same barrier instruction; one warp arriving from
    different pcs is rejected when the barrier completes (UB per spec).
    barrier.sync (non-aligned) allows it;
  * a thread may not arrive twice before the barrier completes;
  * bar.red reduces over the threads that arrived (exited ones have no
    predicate): popc.u32 / and.pred / or.pred. Mixing reductions, or a
    reduction and a plain sync, on one barrier id is rejected.

openassembler/ptx/parse.py.doc:
Minimal PTX parser: one module -> kernels of flat instruction lists.

Covers the syntax our probes and typical ptxas input use: directives, .reg /
.shared / .local / .const / .global declarations (incl. `%r<N>` ranges),
labels, guards, vector operands `{a, b}`, addresses `[reg+off]`, `a|b`
predicate pairs, and immediates (hex, decimal, 0f/0d float bits).

openassembler/ptx/semantics.py.doc: PTX instruction semantics (from the PTX ISA spec).

symbols.name: execute
symbols.doc: Run one instruction for `lanes`; return {next_pc: lanes}.

symbols.name: rd
symbols.doc: Read operand as type t; signed types come back as Python negative ints.

symbols.name: barrier_form
symbols.doc:
Decode the CTA-barrier forms nvcc and hand-written PTX use:
    bar{.cta}.sync a{, b}      barrier{.cta}.sync{.aligned} a{, b}
    bar{.cta}.arrive a, b      barrier{.cta}.arrive{.aligned} a, b
    bar{.cta}.red.popc.u32 d, a{, b}, {!}p
    bar{.cta}.red.{and,or}.pred d, a{, b}, {!}p     (barrier.red likewise)
a = barrier id 0..15, b = thread count (immediate or register, uniform per
warp). __syncthreads() is `bar.sync 0`; __syncthreads_count/_and/_or are the
bar.red forms. Anything else (bare `bar`, .cluster, bar.arrive without a
count, other reduction types) is rejected rather than guessed at.

symbols.name: _bar_warp
symbols.doc:
bar.warp.sync membermask (__syncwarp). The scheduler runs the lowest-pc
lane group first, so any live lane of the mask that is not executing this
instruction with us has diverged past it and would have to arrive later at a
(possibly different) bar.warp.sync -- that rendezvous is not modeled, so it is
rejected instead of treated as a no-op. Exited lanes in the mask are ignored.

openassembler/ptx/semantics_fp.py.doc:
PTX floating-point semantics (exact, via openassembler.emu.fp), plus cvt.

Approximate instructions (rcp/sqrt/rsqrt/ex2/lg2/sin/cos/tanh .approx, div.approx)
have implementation-defined error in the spec. We compute the exact result and
tag it APPROX; the harness compares those lanes with a ulp tolerance instead of
bit-exactly.

symbols.name: _exact_sqrt
symbols.doc: Correctly rounded sqrt: find the representable neighbours of sqrt(q) exactly.

openassembler/pyfront/__init__.py.doc:
openassembler.pyfront: a from-scratch, minimal Python-subset compiler to PTX.

Not a general Python compiler -- a small, explicitly scoped numeric subset
(Numba @cuda.jit-lite), enough to write elementwise ops, reductions, softmax-style
kernels and tiled matmuls with Python syntax instead of raw PTX text:

    @kernel
    def add(a: Array(f32), b: Array(f32), out: Array(f32), n: i32):
        i = tid_x() + ctaid_x() * ntid_x()
        if i < n:
            out[i] = a[i] + b[i]

`compile_file(path)` compiles every top-level @kernel of a file into one PTX module
WITHOUT importing or executing the file; `compile_kernel(fn)` does one kernel (a live
function or a `find_kernel()` result) and produces the identical PTX. The PTX then goes
through the exact same openassembler.backend.ra / openassembler.container.cubin
pipeline as any other PTX in this repo.

Supported: typed params (Array(f32|i32|u32), i32/u32/f32 scalars), local int/float
variables, + - * / // % (Python semantics: / is true division to f32, // and % floor
on ints), comparisons, if/elif/else with and/or/not, for-range and while loops with
break/continue, float()/int(), min/max/abs, sqrt (exact) and approximate
exp/log/tanh/rsqrt (also as math.sqrt/exp/log/tanh), shared_array + syncthreads, array
reads/writes, and tid_x/ctaid_x/ntid_x (and _y/_z). Anything else raises NotSupported
with the line. Every place GPU semantics differ from Python's is listed in the
openassembler.pyfront.compile module docstring.

openassembler/pyfront/compile.py.doc:
The actual Python-subset -> PTX compiler: ast.parse the kernel's source, walk the tree,
emit PTX text. One Python variable name gets exactly one fixed PTX register for its whole
scope (reused across loop iterations and if/else branches, same discipline as the
hand-written PTX elsewhere in this repo) -- no SSA, no phi nodes, by design: this is a
small enough subset that a classic one-register-per-variable allocator is both correct and
trivial to verify.

STATIC COMPILATION. compile_file(path) never imports or executes the user's file: it
ast-parses it, finds the top-level functions decorated @kernel / @pyfront.kernel /
@openassembler.pyfront.kernel, and resolves every name (annotations, intrinsics, `math.`)
from the file's import statements alone. A repo-wide compile therefore cannot run
arbitrary top-level code (tests/test_pyfront_semantics.py compiles a file whose top level
is `raise SystemExit`). find_kernel() is static too; compile_kernel(fn) accepts either a
live function (it re-parses the function's whole source file, so it sees the same imports)
or find_kernel's result, and emits byte-identical PTX to compile_file for the same kernel.

SEMANTICS CONTRACT. The goal is EXACT Python semantics wherever the GPU allows; every
place it can't is listed here (and nothing else is silently different):

  Integers are i32 (two's complement, wrapping). Python ints are unbounded: any i32
  overflow (x * y past 2**31, abs(-2**31), -(-2**31), -2**31 // -1) wraps on the GPU where
  Python would just grow. Integer literals outside i32 are rejected at compile time.
  Floats are f32, not Python's float64: every operation rounds to f32. A single + - * /
  sqrt on f32 inputs is bit-identical to Python computing in float64 and rounding the
  result to f32 (float64 has > 2*24+2 bits, so the double rounding is innocuous), but a
  CHAIN of operations rounds after every step, which Python does not do.
  Float literals are rounded to the nearest f32.

  a / b   true division, always f32 (i32 operands are converted with cvt.rn.f32 first,
          exact for |x| <= 2**24), emitted as div.rn.f32 -- IEEE correctly rounded, so it
          equals Python's a / b rounded to f32. Division by a constant power of two is
          emitted as the (exactly equal) multiply by its reciprocal. Python raises
          ZeroDivisionError for x / 0; the GPU returns +-inf / NaN (IEEE). A literal
          0 or 0.0 divisor is rejected at compile time.
  a // b, a % b on i32: Python FLOOR semantics (-7 // 2 == -4, -7 % 2 == 1,
          7 % -2 == -1, sign of % follows the divisor). Emitted as PTX's truncating
          div.s32 (+ a remainder) and a branch-free floor correction; a constant divisor
          stays an immediate so the backend's divide-by-constant path applies, and a
          positive power-of-two divisor becomes shr.s32 / and.b32 (which ARE floor
          semantics in two's complement). On u32 floor == truncation, so div.u32/rem.u32
          as-is. Division by zero is UNDEFINED on the GPU (Python raises); -2**31 // -1
          wraps. A literal 0 divisor is rejected at compile time.
  a // b, a % b on f32: rejected. Python's float // is floor((a - a % b) / b) computed
          with an exact fmod and special sign/zero/inf rules (e.g. 1 // 0.1 == 9.0 even
          though 1 / 0.1 == 10.0); PTX has no matching instruction and composing one from
          floor(a / b) would be wrong exactly on those edge cases.
  float(x) on i32: cvt.rn.f32.s32 (round to nearest; exact for |x| <= 2**24, Python's
          float() would be exact up to 2**53). int(x) on f32: cvt.rzi.s32.f32, truncation
          toward zero like Python. Python raises for int(nan) / int(inf) and grows past
          2**31; the GPU saturates (NaN -> 0, out-of-range -> -2**31 / 2**31-1).
          int(u32) is rejected (values >= 2**31 don't fit i32).
  min(a, b), max(a, b): two arguments of the same type. i32/u32 -> min/max PTX
          (identical to Python on ints). f32 -> setp + selp mirroring CPython's exact
          algorithm (min returns b only if b < a, else a), so NaN and -0.0/+0.0 order
          behave exactly like Python -- PTX's min.f32 differs on both (it drops NaNs
          and orders -0 < +0). abs(x): i32 as max(x, -x) (abs(-2**31) wraps), f32 as
          abs.f32 (clears the sign bit; NaN payload may be canonicalized).
  sqrt(x) / math.sqrt(x): sqrt.rn.f32, correctly rounded -- exact. sqrt of a negative
          number returns NaN where Python's math.sqrt raises ValueError; sqrt(-0.0) is -0.0
          in both. Denormal inputs are handled exactly (no flush-to-zero).
  exp, log, tanh (bare, or as math.exp / math.log / math.tanh after `import math`) and
          rsqrt are APPROXIMATE, like CUDA's __expf/__logf/tanhf fast paths:
            exp(x)   = ex2.approx.f32(x * log2(e))   (the x*log2(e) rounding grows the
                       error with |x|: CUDA documents 2 + floor(|1.173 x|) ulp
                       for __expf, which is this exact sequence)
            log(x)   = lg2.approx.f32(x) * ln(2)     (CUDA's __logf: abs error <= 2**-21.41 for x in
                       [0.5, 2], <= 3 ulp elsewhere; log(0) = -inf, log(x<0) = NaN where
                       Python raises)
            tanh(x)  = tanh.approx.f32(x)            (relative error ~2**-11, sm_75+)
            rsqrt(x) = rsqrt.approx.f32(x)           (a few ulp; pyfront-only, math has none)
          These are deliberate: they are what training kernels use (softmax, GELU,
          layernorm); an exactly rounded expf is a long software sequence.
  Comparisons: < <= > >= == on f32 are ordered (false on NaN, as in Python); != is
          true on NaN, as in Python (setp.neu). Chained comparisons are rejected.
  Conditions of if/while: comparisons, and/or (short-circuited into branches), `not`
          (folded into the branch polarity -- no predicate is materialized), a bare
          int/float (Python truthiness: != 0, NaN is true), True/False. `not` anywhere
          else (assigned, nested in arithmetic) is rejected; so are and/or used as values.
  Loops: for v in range(start, stop[, step]) with a constant non-zero step, while cond:,
          break and continue in both, nested to any depth. Bounds are evaluated once
          (Python semantics), the loop variable keeps its last value after the loop, and
          assigning to it inside the body does not change the iteration count (both via
          a hidden counter, used only when the variable is assigned in the body or
          read outside the loop). An i32 counter that would overflow (range near 2**31
          with a large step) wraps on the GPU. for/while ... else are rejected.
  Arrays: Array(f32|i32|u32) parameters (global memory), and shared memory declared at
          kernel top level as  s = shared_array(f32, 256)  (i32/u32 too; constant
          positive size; at most 48 KB in total), read/written as s[i]. Indices are i32.
          Out-of-bounds indices are not checked (Python raises IndexError; the GPU
          reads/writes whatever is there) and NEGATIVE indices do not count from the end
          (a constant negative index is rejected; a runtime one is out of bounds).
          Shared memory starts uninitialized (Python code can't observe that only
          because pyfront kernels can't run as Python).
  syncthreads() -> bar.sync 0. Every thread of the block must reach it, so it is rejected
          at compile time when it is (lexically) under control flow that depends on the
          thread index -- an if/while on tid_x(), a for with a tid-dependent bound, or
          after a tid-dependent return/break -- which would deadlock or be undefined.
          The analysis is conservative: values loaded from arrays at a tid-dependent index
          count as thread-dependent too.
  Not supported (NotSupported with the line): any other call, lists/tuples/dicts,
          strings, attribute access other than math./pyfront. intrinsics, augmented or
          plain assignment to more than one target, f16/f64, atomics, recursion, nested
          functions, lambdas, try/with, global/nonlocal. Bitwise operators and ** are
          not implemented.

symbols.name: NotSupported
symbols.doc:
Raised for any Python construct outside the compiled subset, with the source line
(and, from compile_file, the file) attached -- we never guess at semantics we haven't
modeled.

symbols.name: _Names
symbols.doc:
What names in the user's file refer to, read off its import statements only (never
by executing it). resolve() maps an expression to a canonical string:
  "pf.X"   -- openassembler.pyfront's X (from any of: bare X never rebound by an import,
              `from openassembler.pyfront import X [as Y]`, `pf.X` after
              `import openassembler.pyfront as pf`, `openassembler.pyfront.X`, ...)
  "math.X" -- the math module's X (needs an `import math [as m]` / `from math import X`)
  "X"      -- a bare builtin name (min, max, abs, float, int, range) not shadowed
  None     -- anything else.

symbols.name: _resolve_type
symbols.doc:
Resolve a parameter annotation (i32, f32, Array(f32), pf.Array(pf.i32), or the same
as a string under `from __future__ import annotations`) from the AST -- no eval.

symbols.name: _BarrierCheck
symbols.doc:
Rejects syncthreads() under thread-dependent control flow (see the module docstring).
`varying` = names whose value may differ between threads of one block; it is grown to a
fixpoint because loops carry values backwards. Conservative by construction: anything
touched by a tid, by an array read at a varying index, or assigned under varying control
flow is varying.

symbols.name: _Scope
symbols.doc: One kernel's codegen state: register allocation, labels, output.

symbols.name: _const_value
symbols.doc: int/float value of a literal, folding unary +/- (so `-2` is a constant); else None.

symbols.name: _Emitter
symbols.doc:
One pass over the kernel body; every statement either emits PTX or raises
NotSupported. Expressions return a _Reg holding the value (a fresh scratch register
unless the expression is a bare variable read, which returns its home register).

symbols.name: _compile_entry
symbols.doc: One `.visible .entry` (no module header) for a kernel FunctionDef.

symbols.name: _file_kernels
symbols.doc:
Top-level @kernel functions, in file order; duplicate names are an error (Python
would silently keep the last one).

symbols.name: compile_file
symbols.doc:
Compile every top-level @kernel in `path` into ONE PTX module (one header, one
.visible .entry per kernel, in file order) WITHOUT importing or executing the file.
Returns (ptx, kernel names); ("", []) if the file has no @kernel. Errors are
NotSupported naming the file and line.

symbols.name: KernelRef
symbols.doc:
A @kernel found statically in a file by find_kernel (the file was never executed).
Accepted by compile_kernel exactly like the decorated function.

symbols.name: find_kernel
symbols.doc:
Find the @kernel named `entry` in a .py file (or the only one, if entry is None)
WITHOUT importing it -- same static scan as compile_file. Raises NotSupported if none,
or several when entry is None (same "don't guess" policy as the rest of pyfront).

symbols.name: _live_source
symbols.doc:
AST of a live function: parse its WHOLE source file (so the names/imports it sees
are exactly those compile_file would see) and pick the def by line; fall back to the
function's own source text (e.g. defined in a REPL).

symbols.name: compile_kernel
symbols.doc:
PTX (header + one .visible .entry) for one kernel: a @kernel-decorated function, a
plain function, or a find_kernel() result. Byte-identical to the corresponding entry
of compile_file(). Raises NotSupported for anything outside the module docstring's
subset.

symbols.name: kernel
symbols.doc:
Marks a function as pyfront-compilable. Calling it directly in plain Python raises --
use openassembler.pyfront.compile_kernel(fn) to get PTX.

symbols.name: _block
symbols.doc:
Returns (divergent exit that leaves the innermost loop: break/continue,
divergent return). `div` = control flow here already depends on the thread.

symbols.name: var_reg
symbols.doc:
First assignment to `name` allocates its register; later ones must agree on type
-- reassigning a scalar's type is not supported (it would need a second physical
register, defeating the point of reusing one name across branches/iterations).

symbols.name: _jump
symbols.doc: Branch to `label` iff bool(test) == when; otherwise fall through.

symbols.name: _lit_as
symbols.doc:
Materialize literal v. An int literal next to an f32 operand becomes an f32
constant (Python would promote it), but only when that conversion is exact.

symbols.name: _pair
symbols.doc: Evaluate two operands; a literal takes the other side's type (see _lit_as).

symbols.name: _arith
symbols.doc:
left/right: AST nodes or already-evaluated (reg, kind). `into`: write a one-
instruction result straight there (`s += x` stays a single add, as before).

symbols.name: _divconst
symbols.doc: a // d or a % d for a literal d != 0, Python floor semantics.

symbols.name: _divreg
symbols.doc: a // b or a % b, b a register: truncating div + branch-free floor correction.

symbols.name: _compare

is emitted as eq + inverted polarity (our backend has no setp.neu); as a value it
must be setp.neu.f32 -- ordered ne would be wrong (false) on NaN.

symbols.name: _address
