openassembler/runner.py.doc:
`openassembler run` (and the run half of `cnr`): execute already-compiled cubins on
a real GPU, ours next to ptxas's, on identical inputs, and compare bit for bit.

Reads OUTDIR/manifest.json (schema: openassembler.project). For every selected kernel
it builds two GPU jobs in openassembler.gpu.cuda_driver.run_plan_job's format -- one
loading our cubin (cubin/<name>.cubin), one loading the ptxas -O3 reference build of
the same PTX (.build/reference/<name>.cubin) -- with the same buffers, the same
initial data and the same launches. Both run in openassembler.gpu.batch (a worker
subprocess per fault, so one kernel faulting doesn't stop the others), every compared
buffer is read back after the first run and compared byte for byte, then the step
list is timed `reps` times (cuEvents, median reported).

Inputs, two ways:
  * auto-harness (default), like openassembler.verify: every pointer (.u64) param is a
    buffer of N 4-byte elements filled with random f32 data in [-1, 1); integer params
    named n/count/size/len/num/length (any case) are N, other integers are 16 (small:
    they are usually dimensions or strides, and a big one would index past N); float
    params are random. 1-D launch, block 256, grid ceil(N/256). Kernels with a
    different geometry fault or read past the buffers -- that is reported per kernel,
    with the hint to describe the launch with --spec.
  * --spec SPEC.json, for real workloads and multi-kernel pipelines:
      {"buffers": {"x": {"count": 4096, "dtype": "f32", "init": "random"},
                   "y": {"count": 4096, "dtype": "i32", "init": "zeros"},      init: random | zeros | [values...]
                   "w": {"count": 3, "dtype": "u32", "init": [1, 2, 3]}},      dtype: f32 | i32 | u32 (4 bytes each)
       "steps": [{"kernel": "relu", "source": "examples/mlp/kernels.py",      source: only if the name is ambiguous
                  "grid": 16, "block": [256, 1, 1], "smem": 0,                 grid/block: int or [x, y, z]
                  "args": [{"buf": "x"}, {"buf": "y", "offset": 0},            offset in bytes (default 0)
                           {"i32": 4096}, {"u32": 7}, {"f32": 0.5}, {"u64": 1}]}],
       "compare": ["y"],                                                       default: every buffer
       "reps": 20}                                                             default: --reps
    Random i32/u32 data is uniform in [0, count) so it can serve as indices. Each step's
    kernel runs from our cubin in the "ours" job and from the reference cubin in the
    "ptxas" job; a pipeline is one comparison.

Backends: local (this Linux machine's NVIDIA driver), user@host (SSH, like
tools/gpu_run.py: copies only the stdlib-only openassembler/gpu package, a hard remote
`timeout`, results copied back, remote dir removed), modal (openassembler/gpu/modal_app.py
via the `modal` CLI, so modal can live in any Python env). --dry-run never touches a
GPU: it prints the jobs, upload size and (modal) an estimated cost. The last report is
saved to OUTDIR/run.json.

openassembler/verify.py.doc:
A generic correctness check: compile a kernel with our backend, run it on
the SASS emulator, run the same PTX on the reference interpreter, and diff
every pointer-typed parameter's memory afterward.

Unlike openassembler/emu/probe.py (the original probe harness, fixed to one
specific 4-parameter signature), this works for any kernel the pyfront/
cppfront frontends -- or anyone's hand-written PTX -- produce: it reads the
kernel's own `.param` list and launch geometry instead of assuming one.
Trade-off: it doesn't know what each array actually means (is `b` an input
or scratch space?), so every pointer parameter is treated as length `n`
(matching the launch's total thread count) and filled with random data; a
kernel that writes outside that bound needs a hand-written check instead
(same as the original probes' fixed ABI didn't generalize either).

Geometry: by default one CTA of `n_elems` threads (the original behaviour).
With `grid=g` the same n_elems elements are spread over g CTAs of
ceil(n_elems / g) threads, so a kernel indexing with
%ctaid.x * %ntid.x + %tid.x touches every element and really runs several
blocks; `block=` overrides the block size. Each CTA runs separately on both
engines (one Machine / Interp per %ctaid, own shared memory, one shared
global memory) in the same order, which is exact for kernels whose CTAs don't
communicate through global memory within one launch -- the CUDA model gives
no ordering between CTAs anyway.

symbols.name: _rand_scalar
symbols.doc:
A plausible scalar value for a parameter that isn't a pointer. Integer
scalars default to a SMALL bounded range (0..n_elems), not a wide random
range: in virtually any real kernel an integer scalar is a dimension,
loop bound, or index multiplier (batch size, a matrix's inner
dimension, ...), and a large random value here either blows the
emulator's step limit (a loop bounded by it) or reads/writes outside
the n_elems-sized buffers this checker allocates. Floats are data
values, not structural, so they get a wider plausible range.

symbols.name: _align
symbols.doc:
Pad the packed kernel-parameter bytes so the next value starts at a
multiple of its own size -- the layout CUDA (and our backend, see
Selector.param_off) uses. Without it, `(float a, float* x, ...)` puts the
pointer at offset 4 instead of 8 and the kernel reads garbage.

symbols.name: launch_geometry
symbols.doc:
(grid, block) for run_and_diff: block defaults to ceil(n_elems / grid.x)
threads along x (n_elems itself for one CTA, the original behaviour).

Build matching inputs, run both engines, return every differing
(param, index) pair -- empty means bit-exact. `sass_code`/`sass_labels`
are exactly what openassembler.backend.ra.compile_kernel returns.
`grid`/`block`: see the module docstring (defaults: 1 CTA of n_elems).

body is run

  2. as the PTX pyfront emitted, on the reference PTX interpreter,
  3. as the SASS our backend generated (and encoded: every word must have a template),
     on the SASS emulator.
Results are {array name: list}; f32 values compare by bits except that any NaN equals
any NaN (PTX canonicalizes NaN payloads, Python keeps them).

The SASS leg raises Pending (-> pytest.skip) when the backend or the encoder rejects the
kernel: pyfront may emit PTX (div.rn.f32, sqrt.rn.f32, cvt, ex2/lg2.approx, ...) that our
backend learns in a separate change; those legs turn on by themselves once it does.

tests/test_interp_barrier.py.doc:
Cooperative CTA barriers in the PTX reference interpreter (openassembler/ptx/interp.py).

Each shared-memory kernel runs three ways and must agree bit-for-bit:
  1. the PTX interpreter (several warps, bar.sync scheduled cooperatively),
  2. the SASS emulator running ptxas's own SASS for the same PTX (the emulator's
     multi-warp BAR.SYNC is the independent model being cross-checked),
  3. a plain-Python reference of what the kernel computes.
Where our backend (openassembler.backend.ra) compiles the kernel, its SASS is
compared too; where it rejects nvcc's loops, that part is skipped with the reason.
Interpreter-only edge cases (deadlock, divergence, exits, counted barriers,
bar.arrive, multi-warp bar.red) are checked against Python references and the
PTX ISA's rules. Needs ptxas/nvdisasm/nvcc (env/cuda.sh) for the oracle parts.

symbols.name: pack_params
symbols.doc: CUDA param layout: each value at a multiple of its own size.

symbols.name: named
symbols.doc: Params given positionally (nvcc names them <kernel>_param_<i>) -> by name.

symbols.name: ptxas_sass
symbols.doc:
ptxas's own build of kernel `kname` of `ptx` (ptxas -e: only that kernel, so
load_listing needs no kernel filter -- its filter mistakes the .sectionflags
line of a kernel with barriers for a new section), disassembled.

symbols.name: our_sass
symbols.doc: Our backend's SASS for kname, or pytest.skip with the backend's reason.

symbols.name: cuda_ptx
symbols.doc: nvcc --ptx of CUDA_SRC (one nvcc run for the whole module).

symbols.name: three_way
symbols.doc: Interpreter == ptxas SASS on the emulator == Python reference (and our SASS if asked).

symbols.name: hand_rev
symbols.doc:
Hand-written shared-memory reversal of %ntid.x (a power of two) u32 values
around `barrier`: thread i reads slot i ^ (ntid - 1) = ntid - 1 - i. (The XOR
form keeps ptxas from folding a negative LDS offset, `[R0.X4+-0x4]`, which
the emulator's operand parser does not accept yet.)

symbols.name: test_barrier_actually_orders_shared_memory
symbols.doc:
Sanity check that the tests above can fail: with the barrier removed, warp 0
runs to the end before warp 1 stores, so it reads never-written shared memory.

symbols.name: test_nvcc_block_tree_reduction
symbols.doc:
256 floats per block, log2(256) = 8 rounds of `if (i < st) ...; __syncthreads()`,
two blocks. Random floats, so the f32 rounding of the tree order is checked too.

symbols.name: test_nvcc_tiled_matmul
symbols.doc:
32x32 matmul as a 2x2 grid of 16x16 blocks: two tiles per block, two
__syncthreads per tile. Small-integer inputs keep every partial sum exact, so
the reference is independent of nvcc's fma contraction.

symbols.name: test_nvcc_threads_exit_before_barrier
symbols.doc:
128 threads, threads >= n return before __syncthreads(): n=20 leaves whole
warps exited, n=40/100 a partially exited warp. Exited threads count as arrived.

symbols.name: hand_red
symbols.doc:
The bar.red forms nvcc emits for __syncthreads_count/_and/_or (copied from its
PTX, minus the `{ .reg .pred %p1; ... }` scoping blocks the PTX parser doesn't
take yet), plus a negated predicate: out[i] = count*1000 + and*100 + or*10 + nand.

symbols.name: test_bar_red_one_warp
symbols.doc: bar.red on one warp, where the emulator models BAR.RED too: three-way.

symbols.name: test_bar_red_multi_warp
symbols.doc:
Several warps: interpreter vs Python only (the emulator rejects BAR.RED with
more than one warp).

symbols.name: tiny
symbols.doc: out[tid] = %r9 after `body`; %r1 = tid.x, %r2 = ntid.x, %r9 = 0 initially.

symbols.name: test_guard_false_threads_that_exit_count_as_arrived
symbols.doc:
`@%p bar.sync 0` where warp 1's lanes 8..31 skip the barrier and exit: the
barrier still completes (exited threads count as arrived) for the others.

symbols.name: test_same_barrier_from_divergent_paths
symbols.doc:
Odd/even lanes reach barrier 0 at two different instructions. barrier.sync
(non-aligned) is fine per the PTX ISA; bar.sync (= barrier.sync.aligned) is
undefined behaviour there and is refused.

symbols.name: test_deadlock_is_reported_not_hung
symbols.doc: Warp 0 waits at barrier 0, warp 1 at barrier 1: neither can complete.

symbols.name: test_barrier_in_loop_many_rounds
symbols.doc:
A bar.sync inside a uniform 10-iteration loop: 10 completions of barrier 0,
each round reading a slot another warp wrote in the same round.

symbols.name: test_counted_arrive_and_sync
symbols.doc:
Producer/consumer on named barrier 3 with count 64 (CUTLASS-style): the producer
warp stores and bar.arrive's (doesn't wait), the consumer warp bar.sync's and then
reads. Correct whichever warp the interpreter happens to run first.

symbols.name: test_counted_barrier_second_phase_deadlocks
symbols.doc:
Count 64 with three warps all doing bar.sync: warps 0+1 complete phase one, warp 2
alone opens phase two, which can never complete -> reported, not hung.

symbols.name: test_bar_sync_then_bar_red_same_id_sequentially
symbols.doc: A barrier id is free again once it completes: bar.sync 0 then bar.red on 0.

symbols.name: test_run_and_diff_multi_cta_with_barrier
symbols.doc:
run_and_diff on a multi-warp, multi-CTA __syncthreads kernel compiled by our
backend: bit-exact. Also proves the per-CTA %ctaid is wired on both engines:
the reversal is per block, so a wrong ctaid would mismatch.

tests/test_pyfront.py.doc:
openassembler.pyfront: the Python-subset -> PTX compiler. Every kernel here is
checked two ways: against the PTX reference interpreter directly (semantics),
and through our SASS backend + emulator (the actual code path a real build
takes) -- same double-check discipline as the rest of this project.

tests/test_pyfront_semantics.py.doc:
Differential test for openassembler.pyfront: the SAME kernel body is run three ways and
must agree (see tests/pyfront_threeway.py) --
  1. as plain Python (one real thread per GPU thread, the language's real semantics),
  2. as the PTX pyfront emitted, on the reference PTX interpreter,
  3. as the SASS our backend generated, on the SASS emulator.

`compile --verify` only compares (2) with (3), so a bug in the Python -> PTX step (a dropped
`return`, a loop that runs the wrong number of times, truncating instead of floor division)
passes it. The first cases are the silent miscompiles found by auditing the docs; the rest
cover each construct in the module docstring of openassembler/pyfront/compile.py, with the
inputs where Python and naive GPU code disagree (negative operands, NaN, -0.0, denormals).

Leg (3) is skipped with "backend support pending" when our backend/encoder can't compile
the PTX yet (div.rn.f32, sqrt, cvt, ...); legs (1) == (2) must always pass.

symbols.name: test_approximate_intrinsics_within_documented_error
symbols.doc:
exp/log/tanh/rsqrt are .approx (module docstring): the interpreter computes the exact
result of each .approx instruction, so only the documented error budget is compared.

symbols.name: test_i32_multiplication_wraps
symbols.doc: i32 arithmetic wraps (Python ints don't): documented, so pin it.

tests/test_pyfront_static.py.doc: Compilation discovers functions statically without executing a user's module.

tests/test_runner.py.doc: Runner planning and result handling can be tested without contacting a GPU.

tests/test_torchfront.py.doc: Repo-level PyTorch application frontend contracts that do not need a GPU.

tests/test_verify.py.doc:
openassembler.verify: the generic correctness checker (any kernel signature,
not just the probe corpus's fixed out/in/k/kf ABI). Exercised here on a
pyfront kernel, since that's exactly the case the original probe-only
checker couldn't handle (the CLI's own --verify picks this automatically
for non-probe-shaped kernels; see openassembler/cli.py:_verify_compiled).

symbols.name: test_generic_verify_catches_a_real_mismatch
symbols.doc:
Sanity check on the checker itself: corrupt one instruction's opcode
(ld -> different op) and confirm run_and_diff actually reports it,
rather than silently agreeing with itself.

tests/test_word.py.doc: Generic field decoding, checked against real sm_80 words (corpus/sm_80/smoke.cubin).

symbols.name: test_corpus_control_valid
symbols.doc: Every word ptxas emitted satisfies the measured stall/yield rule.

symbols.name: test_corpus_guard_and_cbank
symbols.doc: Guard predicate and constant-bank operands match nvdisasm on every corpus word.

third_party/alphatensor/benchmarking/fac.doc: Factorizations discovered by AlphaTensor and the Strassen^2 factorization.

symbols.name: get_4x4x4_alphatensor_gpu
symbols.doc:
Returns a factorization for fast matrix multiplication on NVIDIA V100 GPUs.

This factorization was discovered by AlphaTensor while optimizing for the
runtime of multiplying two 8192 x 8192 matrices on an NVIDIA V100 GPU in
`float32`.

Returns:
  [3, 16, 49]-shaped array representing a rank-49 factorization of the
  (symmetrized version of the) matrix multiplication tensor T_4 = <4, 4, 4>
  in standard arithmetic.

symbols.name: get_4x4x4_alphatensor_tpu
symbols.doc:
Returns a factorization for fast matrix multiplication on a Google TPUv2.

This factorization was discovered by AlphaTensor while optimizing for the
runtime of multiplying two 8192 x 8192 matrices on a TPUv2 in `bfloat16`.

Returns:
  [3, 16, 49]-shaped array representing a rank-49 factorization of the
  (symmetrized version of the) matrix multiplication tensor T_4 = <4, 4, 4>
  in standard arithmetic.

symbols.name: _get_2x2x2_strassen
symbols.doc: Returns [3, 4, 7] array, representing a rank-7 factorization of T_2.

symbols.name: _product_factors
symbols.doc:
Computes the Kronecker product of `factors1` and `factors2`.

Args:
  factors1: [3, n1**2, R1] factors of a tensor T1
  factors2: [3, n2**2, R2] factors of a tensor T2

Returns:
  [3, n1**2 * n2 ** 2, R1 * R2] factorization of the Kronecker square tensor
  Reshape(kron(RT1, RT2)), where `RT1` and `RT2` are the reshapes of T1 and T2
  into 6-dimensional tensors, and `Reshape` reshapes the tensor back into a
  3-dimensional one.

symbols.name: get_4x4x4_strassen_squared
symbols.doc:
Returns Strassen^2 factorization for fast multiplication of 4x4 matrices.

This factorization is obtained by squaring (recursively applying twice)
Strassen's rank-7 factorization of T_2.

Returns:
  [3, 16, 49]-shaped array representing a rank-49 factorization of the
  (symmetrized version of the) matrix multiplication tensor T_4 = <4, 4, 4>
  in standard arithmetic.

third_party/alphatensor/benchmarking/run.doc:
Reproducing GPU speedup reported in the AlphaTensor paper.

Showing GPU speedup of the provably correct fast matrix multiplication
algorithm discovered by AlphaTensor compared to the Strassen^2 baseline.

You should get around 8.5% speedup for multiplying matrices of size 8192 x 8192
in float32 precision on NVIDIA V100 GPU.

This code requires sudo access to set the GPU clock frequency (to reduce
benchmarking variance).

Ideally this code should be run on a server that is not used by others at the
same time to remove interference.

The code was tested on an n1-standard-96 Google Cloud VM instance with eight
V100 GPUs, Intel Skylake CPU, using the "TensorFlow Enterprise 2.9 (CUDA 11.3)"
image, and with Jax installed by running the following commands:
```bash
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install --upgrade "jax[cuda]" \
  -f https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/jax_releases.html
```

third_party/alphatensor/benchmarking/uti.doc: Utils for working with matrix multiplication tensor factorizations.

symbols.name: block_split
symbols.doc: Splits `matrix` into a `n_rows x n_cols` block matrix.

symbols.name: get_matrix_multiplication_tensor
symbols.doc:
Returns the matrix multiplication tensor T_n.

For n >= 1, T_n is a 3D tensor of shape [n*n, n*n, n*n] representing
- the bilinear operation (A, B) -> (AB)^T where A, B are two [n, n] matrices,
- or equivalently the trilinear operation (A, B, C) -> trace(ABC), where
  A, B, C are three [n, n] matrices.

Args:
  n: Size of the matrix multiplication tensor to be returned.
Returns:
  NumPy array of shape [n^2, n^2, n^2] representing the tensor T_n.

symbols.name: algorithm_from_factors
symbols.doc:
Returns a JAX function implementing the algorithm described by `factors`.

Args:
  factors: Matricized factorization of a matrix multiplication tensor, i.e.
    an array of shape [3, n, n, rank].
Returns:
  Function, which given two block matrices `a` and `b` returns the block
  matrix `c` given by `c = a @ b`.

symbols.name: _get_n_from_factors
symbols.doc:
Computes the matrix multiplication tensor size n based on `factors`.

E.g. when multiplying 2x2 matrices with Strassen, the `factors` are of shape
[4, 7], and this function will return 2.

Args:
  factors: [3, n^2, R] shaped NumPy array representing a factorization of T_n.
Returns:
  n, the size of matrices being multiplied by the algorithm represented by
  `factors`.

symbols.doc: Generates two random NumPy matrices to be multiplied.

symbols.name: _device_put
symbols.doc: Converts NumPy arrays into JAX arrays and sends them to GPU.

symbols.name: _get_baseline_op
symbols.doc: Returns a function that applies `jnp.dot` `n_repeat` times.

symbols.name: _get_factorization_op
symbols.doc: Returns an op that applies the `factors` algorithm `n_repeat` times.

symbols.name: _benchmark_op
symbols.doc: Benchmarks `op` `num_trials` times and returns all timings.

symbols.name: benchmark_jnp_dot
symbols.doc: Benchmarks `jnp.dot`.

symbols.doc: Benchmarks the fast matrix multiplication algorithm given by `factors`.

tools/bench_build.py.doc:
Build benchmark cubins: ptxas vs our compiler (safe and mined schedulers).

    PYTHONPATH=. uv run --no-project python tools/bench_build.py [--arch sm_80]

Writes corpus/<arch>/bench/<variant>@<kernel>.cubin for variants
  ptxas   ptxas -O3
  safe    our compiler, stall 6 after every fixed-latency op
  mined   our compiler, stalls from the mined ptxas latency model
Each of ours is checked in the emulator against the PTX interpreter (random inputs,
poisoned registers) before it is written; failures are reported and skipped.

symbols.name: listing
symbols.doc: Emulator-readable listing for our code (label lines before their instruction).

symbols.name: _reschedule_k
symbols.doc:
Compile PTX kernel k with scheduler `model`; returns (code, labels).
Suffix Y / N: force the yield bit on / off on every instruction (experiment).

tools/bench_kernels.py.doc:
Benchmark kernels (probe ABI: out, in, k, kf) for timing ours vs ptxas on GPUs.

Each kernel loops `k` times (k is the kernel param), so run time is dominated by the
loop body and is easy to compare. Every kernel stores its result so nothing is dead.

    BENCH = {name: ptx_body}  (body inserted into tools/ptx_probes.KERNEL)

tools/bitflip.py.doc:
Bit-flip field discovery: flip each bit of seed words, diff nvdisasm's text.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/bitflip.py sm_80

For each distinct (opcode, form) in corpus/<arch>/pairs.jsonl we take one seed
word, produce 128 single-bit variants, and disassemble everything in one batch.
Each bit is classified as:

  invalid    nvdisasm rejects the word        -> constraint bit
  none       text unchanged                   -> unused / control / don't-care
  opcode     base mnemonic changed            -> opcode-space bit
  mod        a mnemonic modifier changed      -> modifier field bit
  guard      the @P guard changed
  op<k>      operand k changed                -> operand field bit

Adjacent bits with the same class form a candidate field. Results go to
specs/<arch>/bitflip.json (machine-readable) and print as a summary.

symbols.name: normalize
symbols.doc:
Raw-mode branch targets are absolute (addr + 16 + offset); make them relative
so a variant at batch slot k compares equal to the seed at slot j.

symbols.name: runs
symbols.doc: Group adjacent bits with the same class into (lo, width, class).

tools/build_corpus.py.doc:
Build corpus/<arch>/: probe PTX -> cubin -> (word, text) pairs.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/build_corpus.py sm_80 [sm_86 sm_90 ...]

Outputs per arch:
  ptx/<probe>.ptx, cubin/<probe>.cubin   generated, never edited
  failed.txt                             probes ptxas rejected, with its message
  pairs.jsonl                            {"probe","addr","word" (hex), "text"} per instruction

tools/compile_check.py.doc:
M3 gate (v0): compile probes with OUR compiler, validate with nvdisasm, check
semantics with the SASS emulator against the PTX interpreter.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/compile_check.py [--only SUBSTR]

Pipeline per probe: PTX -> openassembler.backend.compile -> encode -> splice into the
ptxas cubin's ELF (REGCOUNT / EXIT offsets patched) -> nvdisasm must accept it
and print back exactly our text -> emulator(our SASS) == PTX interpreter.
Also reports our instruction count vs ptxas's (excluding trailing BRA/NOP).

tools/diff_emu.py.doc:
Differential harness: SASS emulator (on ptxas output) vs PTX interpreter.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/diff_emu.py [sm_80] [--trials N] [--only SUBSTR]

For each probe: random inputs (mixing edge values) -> run both -> compare the
8 output bytes per thread. Lanes where the PTX result is spec-undefined are
skipped; lanes whose result came from an `.approx` op are compared within a
ulp tolerance. Writes corpus/<arch>/diff_report.json and prints a summary.

tools/div_const_survey.py.doc:
Survey: how does ptxas lower integer division/remainder by a compile-time constant?

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/div_const_survey.py [sm_80]

For each (op, type, divisor) we compile a probe whose divisor is a PTX immediate,
then classify the SASS:
  shift     power of two handled with shifts/LOP3 only
  magic     multiply-high sequence (IMAD.HI / IMAD.WIDE), no MUFU/I2F/F2I
  runtime   reciprocal computed at run time (I2F + MUFU.RCP + F2I + Newton)
  call      calls an internal helper (64-bit slow path)
Writes corpus/<arch>/div_const_survey.json and docs/findings-div-const.md data table.

tools/fastmm_build.py.doc:
Build the fast-matmul kernels with ptxas and with our compiler (PTX -> SASS -> cubin).

    PYTHONPATH=. python3 tools/fastmm_build.py [--arch sm_80] [--variant opt]

Writes corpus/<arch>/fastmm/{ptxas,ours}@<kernel>.cubin for sgemm64 and lincomb1..8.
Ours = openassembler.backend (no ptxas involved in code generation; ptxas's cubin is only used
as the ELF container template, as for every other kernel we build). Each of ours is
checked in the emulator against a Python reference before it is written:
  sgemm64   64 x 64 x 16, small-integer inputs (exact in f32), 256 threads, poisoned regs
  lincombK  one 4 x 1024 block, random inputs vs f32 evaluation in the same order

symbols.name: check_fgemm
symbols.doc:
128 x 128 x 16 step with small-integer data and coefficients (all exact in f32):
C_o (pre-filled) += w_o (sum u_s A_s)(sum v_t B_t).

symbols.name: params_layout
symbols.doc: PTX param list -> struct format (natural alignment), to cross-check check_*().

tools/fastmm_import.py.doc:
One-time import of AlphaTensor's factorizations into a numpy-free spec file.

    uv run --no-project --with numpy python tools/fastmm_import.py
    -> specs/fastmm/schemes.json.gz   (sparse: per scheme, nonzeros of u, v, w)

factorizations_r.npz stores pickled object arrays, so numpy is needed once; everything
else (openassembler.fastmm) reads the spec with the stdlib. w is converted from AlphaTensor's
C^T indexing (k*n+i) to row-major C (i*p+k); openassembler.fastmm.factors.verify() re-checks
every scheme exactly.

tools/fastmm_run.py.doc:
Run fast-matmul plans (AlphaTensor / Strassen / naive blocks / one big GEMM) on a GPU.

    PYTHONPATH=. python3 tools/fastmm_run.py --dry-run                 # list plans, no GPU
    modal run tools/fastmm_run.py --n 4096 --gpu A100-40GB             # check + time
    modal run tools/fastmm_run.py --n 4096 --schemes at_gpu_4x4x4,strassen_2x2x2

Every plan is run with the kernels compiled by ptxas AND by our compiler (cubins from
tools/fastmm_build.py). Correctness: C is copied back once and compared on the host with
a float64 reference on 64 sampled rows (relative error ||C - C_ref|| / (||A|| ||B||)),
so a wrong plan or a wrong kernel is caught, not just timed. Timing: median of --reps
runs of the whole launch sequence (cuEvents), random order, several rounds.

Billing: one container, max_containers=1, timeout = budget + 60 s, ephemeral app.

symbols.name: _check_data
symbols.doc:
Only what the host check needs, streamed through the same generator as
cuda_driver.rand_f32 (identical values, rounded to f32): the sampled rows of A and the
checked columns of B. Holding all of A and B as Python floats took ~4 GB at n = 8192
and starved Modal's client heartbeat (the app was stopped mid-run).

symbols.name: check
symbols.doc: Relative Frobenius error on the sampled rows x 128 columns, float64 reference.

tools/fit_mma.py.doc:
Fit the tensor-core accumulation model to recorded A100 outputs (offline, $0).

    PYTHONPATH=. uv run --no-project python tools/fit_mma.py corpus/sm_80/gpu_a100_40gb_tensor.raw.json.gz

The mma probes (tools/ptx_probes.py) compute, per thread,
    A = {r1, r2, r3, r4}, B = {r1, r2}, C = {f1, f2, f3, f1}   (f = bit-cast of r)
and store D elements 0 and 3. So from the recorded inputs we rebuild the full
A, B, C matrices with the PTX fragment layouts and compare candidate models of
the hardware's dot-product unit against the GPU's bits, without the emulator.

Model family (Fasi et al. 2021 style): products are exact; per block of `block`
products the terms and the running accumulator are aligned to the largest
exponent, each truncated to `bits` bits below it, summed exactly, then rounded
to f32 with `round`. tf32 inputs are reduced from f32 by `tf32_in`.

symbols.name: matrices
symbols.doc: Rebuild A, B, C (values) from one trial's per-thread inputs.

symbols.name: model_dot

tools/fit_mma_nominal.py.doc:
Fit the tensor-core accumulation model with NOMINAL-exponent alignment (the model
that matches the A100 on 100% of lanes; see openassembler/emu/tensor.py MMA_MODEL).

    PYTHONPATH=. uv run --no-project python tools/fit_mma_nominal.py

tools/gpu_bisect.py.doc:
Build the cubin variants used to find why our cubins faulted on the A100.

    PYTHONPATH=. uv run --no-project python tools/gpu_bisect.py elf      # -> corpus/sm_80/bisect
    PYTHONPATH=. uv run --no-project python tools/gpu_bisect.py regs     # -> corpus/sm_80/bisect5
    modal run tools/gpu_modal.py --which dir:corpus/sm_80/bisect  --trials 2 --budget 120
    modal run tools/gpu_modal.py --which dir:corpus/sm_80/bisect5 --trials 1 --budget 200

elf:  ptxas cubins rewritten by our ELF writer (same bytes / grown .text / raised
      register count / re-encoded words). All matched on A100: the writer is sound.
regs: ptxas's add.s32.r kernel plus one inserted `MOV Rd, R6`, for many Rd and
      declared register counts n. Result (gpu_a100_40gb_bisect5.json): faults with
      CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION iff n < Rd + 3  ->  openassembler.container.cubin.required_regcount.
Each file is "<variant>@<kernel>.cubin"; gpu_common checks it against the emulator
running ptxas's SASS for <kernel>.

tools/gpu_common.py.doc:
Local half of GPU validation, shared by every transport (Modal, SSH, local).

build_jobs():   choose cubins + random inputs (same generator as tools/diff_emu.py)
compare():      GPU outputs vs SASS emulator (on the same ptxas cubin) and vs the
                PTX interpreter; classifies every probe and writes JSON.

Probe sets:
  ptxas   corpus/<arch>/cubin/*.cubin    (validates the emulator and our hypotheses)
  ours    corpus/<arch>/ours/*.cubin     (cubins produced by OUR compiler)

symbols.name: _finite
symbols.doc:
Finite value bits with exponents spread enough to exercise alignment/rounding:
70% in [2^-6, 2^6], 25% in [2^-20, 2^20], 5% exact small integers / zero.

symbols.name: structured_inputs
symbols.doc:
Per-thread 4 x u32 inputs whose bit patterns are meaningful for `probe`,
or None to use the generic random generator.

symbols.name: build_jobs
symbols.doc:
which: "ptxas" | "ours" | "dir:<path>". A dir holds files named
"<variant>@<kernel>.cubin"; each is checked against the emulator running
ptxas's SASS for <kernel> (any correct cubin must compute the same thing).

symbols.name: compare
symbols.doc: gpu_res: {job index: {out|error, attrs, oob_bytes}}

symbols.name: report_times
symbols.doc:
Timing table: per kernel, per variant (file prefix before '@'), median ms and
speed-up vs ptxas. Writes JSON next to the correctness result.

tools/gpu_modal.py.doc:
Run probe cubins on a Modal GPU and compare with our emulator + the PTX spec.

    modal run tools/gpu_modal.py --dry-run                  # count jobs + cost estimate, no GPU
    modal run tools/gpu_modal.py --only add.s32 --trials 2  # smoke test (~30 s of A100)
    modal run tools/gpu_modal.py                            # all ptxas probes on A100-40GB
    modal run tools/gpu_modal.py --which ours               # cubins built by OUR compiler

Billing safety (Modal bills a container from start to exit):
  * `modal run` is an ephemeral app: it stops when this local process exits.
    If the local process is killed hard, run `modal app list` and
    `modal app stop <id>` to be sure nothing is left running.
  * Three layers of timeouts: per-job watchdog in openassembler.gpu.batch (kills a
    hung kernel's worker), a global --budget inside the container, and
    Modal's function `timeout` (hard kill) = BUDGET_S + 60 s.
  * One container does the whole batch: one cold start, then jobs back to back.

The container gets only the stdlib-only `openassembler.gpu` package and the jobs
pickle; the emulator / PTX-spec comparison happens locally.

tools/gpu_replay.py.doc:
Replay recorded GPU outputs against the current emulator (offline, no GPU, $0).

    PYTHONPATH=. uv run --no-project python tools/gpu_replay.py corpus/sm_80/gpu_a100_40gb_tensor.raw.json.gz
    ... --only mma.f16 --show 3

Every Modal/SSH run writes <result>.raw.json.gz (inputs + per-thread GPU outputs).
This re-runs the emulator on exactly those inputs, so emulator changes can be checked
against hardware without paying for another run.

tools/gpu_run.py.doc:
Run probe cubins on a GPU you reach over SSH (or on this machine), then compare.

    python tools/gpu_run.py --ssh user@host [--only add] [--trials 4]
    python tools/gpu_run.py --local            # this machine has an NVIDIA GPU + driver

Same jobs, same remote code (stdlib-only openassembler.gpu), and same comparison as
tools/gpu_modal.py. Only the transport differs:
  1. build jobs locally -> jobs.pkl
  2. copy openassembler/__init__.py + openassembler/gpu/ + jobs.pkl to host:/tmp/openassembler_gpu_<pid>
  3. ssh: `timeout <budget+60> python3 -m openassembler.gpu.batch jobs.pkl res.pkl`
     (GNU timeout = hard kill on the remote side even if ssh drops)
  4. copy res.pkl back, delete the remote directory, compare locally
Remote needs: Linux, NVIDIA driver (libcuda.so.1), python3 >= 3.8. No CUDA toolkit.

tools/lat_sweep.py.doc:
Measure fixed-pipeline read-after-write latencies on real hardware.

    PYTHONPATH=. python3 tools/lat_sweep.py                 # -> corpus/sm_80/latsweep
    modal run tools/gpu_modal.py --which dir:corpus/sm_80/latsweep --trials 3 --budget 200
    PYTHONPATH=. python3 tools/lat_sweep.py --report corpus/sm_80/gpu_a100_40gb_latsweep.json

Each kernel is a producer immediately followed by a consumer of its result in a given
operand slot. Our compiler builds it; then the producer's stall is set to s = 1..8 and
one cubin per s is written ("s<s>@<kernel>.cubin"). The GPU result is compared with the
emulator (which has no timing): the smallest s that matches on every lane is the real
latency for (producer, consumer slot). ptxas's mined minimum distances turned out not to
be safe latencies (IMAD -> LOP3 at 4 cycles gave wrong results on the A100).

tools/mine_latency.py.doc:
M2: extract ptxas's machine model from its control codes.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/mine_latency.py [sm_80] [--corpus DIR ...]

For straight-line code (within a basic block), for every register RAW dependency
producer -> consumer:
  * if the consumer waits on a scoreboard the producer set   -> "variable latency" op
  * otherwise the issue distance (sum of stall counts from producer up to, not
    including, the consumer) is a fixed-latency guarantee ptxas relies on.
The minimum distance seen per producer class is ptxas's latency for that class.

Also reports the scoreboard policy (which SB index each op class uses for writes
and reads) and how often scoreboards are shared.
Writes corpus/<arch>/machine_model.json.

symbols.name: defs_uses
symbols.doc: Destination operands: leading Reg/Pred operands, except for stores/branches/etc.

symbols.name: blocks
symbols.doc: Yield basic blocks as lists of insns (split at labels and after control flow).

tools/mlp_build.py.doc:
Build the 2-layer MLP forward-pass kernels (examples/mlp/kernels.py --
linear1, relu, linear2) with ptxas and with our own compiler, for every
optimization level. Each of ours is checked against the PTX reference
interpreter (openassembler.verify.run_and_diff) before being written, same
discipline as tools/fastmm_build.py and tools/bench_build.py.

    PYTHONPATH=. python3 tools/mlp_build.py [--arch sm_80] [--variant opt]

Writes corpus/<arch>/mlp/{ptxas,ours}@<kernel>.cubin.

tools/mlp_run.py.doc:
Run the 2-layer MLP forward pass (examples/mlp/kernels.py: linear1 -> relu
-> linear2) on a real GPU through Modal, with both ptxas- and our-compiler-
built cubins (tools/mlp_build.py), and compare timing + correctness.

    modal run tools/mlp_run.py --dry-run                      # job count + cost, $0
    modal run tools/mlp_run.py --batch 256 --in-dim 512 --hidden 2048 --out-dim 512

Correctness: every run's output is checked against a pure-Python float64
reference (no numpy) on every element -- small enough matrices that this is
cheap, and it means "the MLP forward pass runs correctly on real hardware"
is backed by an independent reference, not just internal agreement between
our two compilers. Timing: median of --reps runs of the 3-launch sequence,
several shuffled rounds (same "a fixed order biases results" lesson as
tools/gpu_modal.py --timing; see docs/STATUS.md "Timing method").

symbols.name: _split_cols
symbols.doc:
n columns -> (block.x, grid.y) so block.x * grid.y >= n and
block.x <= max_block (well under CUDA's 1024-thread/block cap; 256 keeps
occupancy reasonable for linear1/linear2's register use).

symbols.name: _reference
symbols.doc: Pure-Python float64 forward pass -- independent of both compilers.

tools/nn_study.py.doc:
Compile and measure eight NN/transformer operations before optimization changes.

python tools/nn_study.py --dry-run
python tools/nn_study.py --backend modal --budget 180 --rounds 3 --reps 20

Uses one GPU container, shuffled jobs, deterministic inputs, explicit launch specs,
bitwise ptxas comparisons, and timestamped JSON evidence. This is a kernel study,
not an end-to-end training benchmark. No optimizer is changed by this script.

tools/predict_stall.py.doc:
M2 gate: predict ptxas's stall counts from a mined machine model.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/predict_stall.py [sm_80]

Model (in-order issue simulation per basic block):
  issue(k+1) = max( issue(k) + 1,
                    issue(i) + L(i)            for fixed-latency producers i of k+1's sources,
                    issue(p) + occ(pipe)       for the last instruction p on k+1's pipe )
  stall(k)   = issue(k+1) - issue(k)
L comes from corpus/<arch>/machine_model.json (min distance ptxas ever used).
Pipe occupancy is mined too: the min stall ptxas puts between two independent
instructions on the same pipe.

Reports exact-match accuracy of the predicted stall field per instruction class.

symbols.name: mine_occupancy
symbols.doc: Min stall between consecutive *independent* instructions on the same pipe.

symbols.name: mine_min_gap
symbols.doc:
Min stall ptxas ever puts on the instruction *before* a given consumer class
(independent pair). Captures issue constraints of the consumer's pipe, e.g.
S2R / LDG / MUFU need >= 2 cycles after the previous issue.

tools/prove_divconst.py.doc:
Generate and z3-prove multiply-high replacements for div/rem by constants.

Usage: uv run --no-project --with z3-solver==4.15.3.0 python tools/prove_divconst.py [N_RANDOM]
Compares instruction counts against ptxas 12.8 (corpus/sm_80/div_const_survey.json).

tools/ptx_probes.py.doc:
Generate PTX probe kernels that cover the SASS instruction space.

Each probe is one small kernel. Inputs come from global memory (so ptxas
can't constant-fold), one operand optionally comes from a kernel param (which
ptxas turns into a c[0x0][...] operand) or an immediate, and results are stored
back so nothing is dead. Body snippets see these registers:

  %r1..%r4  b32 inputs        %f1..%f3  f32 (bit-cast of %r1..%r3)
  %rd6 %rd7 b64 inputs        %fd1 %fd2 f64 (bit-cast of %rd6 %rd7)
  %rk       b32 kernel param  %fk       f32 kernel param
  %rd4      global input ptr (thread's 16-byte slot)
  %rd5      global output ptr; bytes 0..7 are the result, 8..15 are scratch for store probes
  %r0       %tid.x

and must leave the result in %r10 (and optionally %r11).

symbols.name: probes
symbols.doc: Yield (name, body, needs_shared) for every probe valid on `target`.

symbols.name: module
symbols.doc: One standalone PTX module holding one probe kernel.

tools/ptxas_fragments.py.doc:
Freeze ptxas's SASS for single PTX ops into openassembler/backend/ptxas_fragments.json.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/ptxas_fragments.py [--only KEY]   (needs ptxas + nvdisasm)

For each op (div.rn.f32, rcp.approx.ftz.f32, div.s32, cvt.rmi.f32.f32, ...): build the
standard probe kernel (tools/ptx_probes.py ABI: inputs from a 16-byte global slot per
thread, result stored as 8 bytes), compile with ptxas -arch=sm_80, disassemble, and cut
out the op's code:
  * drop the probe scaffolding: R1 setup, S2R/IMAD.WIDE.U32 address arithmetic, ULDC,
    LDG/STG, EXIT, BSSY/BSYNC, padding;
  * inputs = the registers the LDG wrote (by word), output = the register the STG stored;
  * CALL.REL.NOINC sub / RET.REL.NODEC Rx become plain branches (sub entered by BRA,
    left by BRA to a label after the call site) -- the return-address MOVs then die and
    are removed by a liveness DCE over the fragment's CFG, like every other dead def;
  * branch threading (BRA to BRA, @P BRA a; BRA b; a: -> @!P BRA b) on the result.
Every instruction kept is ptxas's text verbatim (registers are renamed per use site by
the backend). The whole ptxas listing is stored too, so tests can run ptxas's own code
on the emulator offline and compare it with ours.

symbols.name: listing
symbols.doc: nvdisasm -hex output -> [("label", name) | ("insn", text, word)] (labels kept).

symbols.name: _normalize_calls
symbols.doc:
Inline each helper called by the probe body, replacing CALL/RET with BRA.

The common out-of-line helpers are leaf routines. Refuse nested calls rather
than emit a fragment with behavior we did not model.

symbols.name: _slice_rows
symbols.doc:
Backward dataflow slice for the probe result, retaining branches that can
reach result-producing code. The input vector load is a boundary: its live
register words become the fragment's arguments. Output pointer/address uses
are deliberately excluded from the store root.

tools/reencode_cubin.py.doc:
End-to-end check of encoder + cubin writer: text -> words -> cubin -> nvdisasm.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/reencode_cubin.py [sm_80]

For every corpus cubin: re-encode each instruction of each .text section from its
*disassembly text* (plus control bits), splice the words into a copy of the cubin
with our ELF writer, then disassemble the copy with nvdisasm and compare the text.
Kernels with any refused instruction keep the original word for that slot and are
counted as partial.

tools/sb_policy.py.doc:
Scoreboard (dependency barrier) policy of ptxas, and how much it over-waits.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/sb_policy.py [sm_80]

For each wait on scoreboard b at instruction j, the "needed" producers are the
in-flight variable-latency instructions that set b and whose result (write SB)
or source registers (read SB) instruction j actually touches.
  false wait:   j waits on b but none of b's in-flight producers is needed by j
  merged wait:  b has >1 in-flight producer, j needs only some of them
                (j is forced to wait for the slowest one)
Straight-line (per basic block) analysis; cross-block waits are counted separately.

tools/verify_divconst_exhaustive.py.doc:
Exhaustive proof of div/rem-by-constant sequences over all 2^32 inputs.

Usage: uv run --no-project python tools/verify_divconst_exhaustive.py [--jobs 8]

z3 times out on 64-bit multiply-high with non-power-of-two constants, so for
32-bit operations we prove by exhaustion instead: each sequence is compiled to C
(host clang -O3) and compared with C's own / and % on every x in [0, 2^32).
That is a complete proof for 32-bit operands. Writes corpus/sm_80/divconst_proofs.json.

symbols.name: _find_cc
symbols.doc:
The exhaustive check compiles a tiny C program that loops over all 2^32 inputs, so it
needs a C compiler: clang, gcc or cc, whichever the machine has (macOS ships clang; most
Linux installs have gcc).
